maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY

speechtext: The House resumed from Friday, March 25, consideration of the motion of Mr. Chev-rier for the second reading of Bill No. 78, respecting the Montreal, Ottawa and Georgian Bay Canal Company, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Guthrie.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
I feel
rather bashful and nervous, following the ho*, member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) who gave such a wonderful display of eloquence and fluency of language. Although I do not agree with his ideas I think I should congratulate him sincerely upon his vocabulary and the able delivery that marked his speech on Tuesday and Friday evenings. Words upon words came from the lips of the hon. member with such ease as to remind me of a

Georgian Bay Canal Company
gentle rivulet winding through a meadow in a narrow and shallow bed. Or, to change the simile, he clothed his ideas in an exterior of simple dignity so that on the surface they were attractive, but underneath there was no mistaking the fact that he was a true Tory; and although he himself is an able man it must be admitted that he serves a shallow and narrow cause, the cause of Toryism. One not acquainted with Tory inconsistency might well have been surprised the other day to find an hon. gentleman so wroth against insinuations and personalities, but he himself excelled in these. He intimated on rising that his purpose was to refute the insinuations that had characterized the speech of the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Chev-rier), and one had a right at least to expect that in his own speech he would have refrained from making insinuations. That however was not the case. The first part of his speech conveyed the unwarranted insinuation that the Prime Minister of this country (Mr. Mackenzie King) had engaged himself to renew this charter because of the electoral merits of the promoters. I do not wish to speak for the Prime Minister, but inasmuch as that strange suggestion caused so much hilarity I think it might be well to recall it to the House and ask hon. members to consider it. The hon. member painted his picture in such vivid colours that we visualized the Prime Minister listening to the Squire of Newmarket and then finding it impossible to vote against a renewal of the charter.
Sir, the picture represents a very vivacious image of what might be reality. But it is not reality; it is only fiction invented by the hon. member himself. And in view of his wonderful gift in this direction and the unlimited resources of his imagination, one is reminded of those lines from Gray's Elergy:
Full many a flower is born to blush unseen
And waste its sweetness on the desert air.
The rest of his speech was either an insinuation or a fallacious assertion that in voting against the amendment we on this side were playing the game of politics. We are giving 200 miles of lakes and rivers without receiving a dollar in return, spoliating the rights of Ontario and Quebec, and violating the great principle of public ownership. That is what the hon. gentleman says. Let me say that although I am not a lawyer, I shall not be deceived too easily by a member of that profession. In voting against the amendment we are not granting anything; we are not renewing the charter; we are not spoliating provincial rights, and we are not violating the principle of public ownership; we are

simply declaring that in the opinion of the House the bill should go to the committee on railways and canals. As a matter of fact, all we are doing is to refuse to kill the bill at this stage, without that careful consideration which it ought to 'receive from the committee.
In order to make clear what my attitude is on this question, and what I gather to be the attitude of my colleagues, let me assure the House that we stand for no particular group of capitalists; we are not favouring either the Siftons or the Aldreds or the Grausteins. We are not opposed to public ownership in favour of private enterprise; we stand on the side of the government because we want a fair deal given everyone.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext: Which side is the government on?

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
I repeat, we want everyone
to get a square deal, and with that end in view we think that every project which is suggested for the purpose of contributing to a solution of our national problems should be very carefully considered. And the pro-73sal for the construction of the Georgian bay canal, and the development of power alung that route, is one of very great importance which deserves the close scrutiny of the people's representatives. That is my stand on this question, as I believe it is the stand my colleagues take. We firmly believe that if the bill were sent to the committee it could be better investigated than it can possibly be here. Now, what is the real objection to referring the bill to the committee? Is the bill of no importance? Obviously not, because the very fact that this House has spent so much time discussing it is proof that it concerns a matter of serious moment to the country. What then is the cause of the great opposition which it has encountered? It is this: that another private group is seeking for the rights of the Carillon 'power, and such is the situation that if the amendment is carried that private group will remain sole proprietor of the Carillon site. The House ought to consider this point carefully. The hon. member for West Calgary, the other day, gave the House the impression that if the amendment carried and the bill were rejected, the principle of public ownership would be vindicated. That is not so. Let me quote from the hon. member's speech:
Unless this parliament intervenes, the rights of this canal and power enterprise expire on the first day of May and the rights and privileges of this private power company also expire on the first day of May. What then is the duty of parliament? Far be it from me to

Georgian Bay Canal Company
suggest what that duty should be for others. What is my duty? My duty is, so far as my vote and voice are concerned, to see to it that this parliament gives no new life to an enterprise that we would not in this day create if we were called upon to do so, and that we leave the river Ottawa free, by permitting this charter to lapse and by refusing to renew the license to the private company, reserving the vested rights of the owners of the 250 horsepower development.
This is not correct; there is another lease which was granted in 1913, which does not expire until 1974.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
For what
horse-power?

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
For 250 horse-power. But
I would remind the hon. member that the private group owning that lease claim to be in the position of a lessee in possession, and that they have the sole authority to develop power on the Carillon site.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext: Only to the amount called for by their charter; unless they get additional authority they are limited to that.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
I am ready to be corrected
if I am wrong, but this group claim that they possess the sole authority to develop electrical power in that region, and that no one else can proceed with a development of that kind on a large scale until 1974. Of course the Conservative members have well hidden that aspect of the case; they have not spoken of it, and their position in opposition to the renewal of this charter is well understood by everyone. It is only natural that this should be the case, because they gave to the company the leases which it obtained in the past. It would seem that they are interested in the company, according to the facts by which we may judge. In 1913 they gave this lease to the National Hydro; in 1921, at the time of the election, that lease was renewed with greater powers, and in 1926 it was renewed again.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
Surely my hon. friend
will be fair enough also to say that the lease was granted originally in 1909, and renewed in 1928-24 by the government of which he is a supporter.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
Because we stand in this case for a loyal and careful investigation of the matter; because we think it our duty to practise the virtue of justice and to safeguard the public interest and the general welfare of this country, the gallant knights backing the opposition to this bill have attacked us in various manners. They have insinuated that we were willing to violate the principle of
public ownership and to despoil well-determined provincial rights; they, have accused us cf playing the game of politics and have depicted the Prime Minister as having made his decision on this bill on the electoral merits of the promoters. But against me personally they have come out with the most insidious attacks. The National Hydro has asked each municipality in my constituency to send in to the government the following resolution:
Moved by . . . , , seconded by ... . that the council of the municipality of. . . . respectfully urges the parliament of Canada not to renew the charter of the Montreal, Ottawa and Georgian Bay Canal Company, known as Bill No. 78, as in our opinion this bill is not in the interests of the province of Ontario as it is an attempt to deprive the people of this province of their right to the powers to be developed from the waters of the Ottawa river; and further, that this charter has been in existence for thirty-three years, and no actual construction has taken place, and we believe the renewal of this charter would be contrary and prejudicial to the public interest.
But that is not all. The newspapers of my constituency have also attacked' me, with the exception of the Prescott and Russell Advocate of L'Orignal. I quote from the Eastern Ontario Review, published at Van-kleek Hill, the following open letter to myself :
An Open Letter to Mr. L. Auger, M.P.
For Prescott County as to His Position on the Georgian Bay Canal Scheme
Dear Mr. Auger,
Your silence in parliament and moreover your reported disappearance; also the published information of the number of letters you have received from the fair sex all over the country, and the reputed number of marriage offers tendered you, has led us to wonder what you are doing in parliament.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
The letter continues:
No doubt you are aware that the county of Prescott has sent you to parliament for the good of the people of this historical county, not to further your own popularity with the fair sex. Just now a matter of vital importance is before the House of Commons, that is, the granting of another charter to the Georgian bay canal. Eight times has this question appeared, and eight times has been talked out. One division has taken place and Mr. Auger did not vote, nor was he paired. Now our youthful and handsome young member knows that if the Georgian bay canal scheme goes through that it sounds the death knell of the Carillon power development situated in the eastern corner of Prescott county and which would necessitate the spending of millions in our midst. What is his position? Does he intend to stand by Carillon or Georgian bay canal? No two ways about it. County of Prescott and its welfare versus the Sifton interests.

Georgian Bay Canal Company
Another article of the same nature appeared in t'he same newspaper on Friday of last week. These insinuations are stupid, malicious and clumsy, but one is bound to sympathize with their author for his lack of common sense. One is also amused, because through his human cloak appears the ears and fur of the silly ass; nothing should be said in reply to this except that the man is entirely-and willingly-in error, and that he has a cause to serve which he does not openly avow. The attacks made against myself because I have not been active in working against the Georgian bay canal scheme are most unjust and unwarranted; they are not fair, because we can justify the stand W'e take on the amendment. We must vote against the amendment for several reasons, first that by so voting we do not grant anything, we do not accept the principle of private enterprise nor do we vote against the principle of public ownership. We do not grant a charter; we do not give away 200 miles of waterway; we give nothing to anyone. We simply desire carefully to study this scheme which is of such importance to the people of this country, and I believe that the people of Canada are sufficiently interested to desire that such a study be made. It appears that a vote for the amendment is only a vote in favour of the National Hydro, and not a vote for the principle of public ownership or the protection of provincial rights. I submit, therefore, that we have ample reason to vote against the amendment.
I think the project most important, because if the canal should be built it would mean greater facility of transportation. The fact has been demonstrated that the construction of this canal would mean a saving of time, of distance and of money in the transportation of goods from the west to the east, and from the east to the west. Its construction would result in greater facility of transportation which would help to solve one of our greatest national problems. It would help also to create a Canadian market about which our Conservative friends are continually talking. In my opinion improved transportation facilities would be more effective in building up a Canadian market than any action we could take through the medium of a tariff policy. Improved transportation would also widely advertise this country abroad. It would help to attract immigration which heretofore has been going to the United States. The republic to the south has always attracted foreign immigrants because that country has a reputation for planning and executing great works. Labourers flock there because the}' are reasonably sure of getting employment.

If this canal were constructed it would result-in such publicity for Canada as to accomplish quicker results than could be achieved through the action of immigration agents in London and other cities of the world. The construction of this work would also stimulate industry and commerce. The ordinary mind can scarcely grasp the benefits it would bring about; it would take an imagination like that of the hon. member for West Calgary to visualize them.
In concluding my remarks, let me quote not from a foreign source but from an hon. member sitting on this side of the House:
My hope in sending this matter to the committee, would be that from that committee might come some constructive proposition that would help us to deal properly with a great national problem.
This was the view expressed by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown). Further on in the same speech the hon. gentleman said:
I take the position that we should send this bill to the committee, only in the hope that from the committee will come some suggestion to enable us to settle the question in the interests of the Dominion, whose rights in this great waterway are paramount.
And again:
I am satisfied, Mr. Speaker, that this could be so done as to secure the end that we have in view-that these great natural resources shall be preserved and developed in such a way as to secure the maximum benefit for the great mass of the common people of Canada.
These observations of the hon. member for Lisgar, to my mind, contain an expression of sound Liberalism and true patriotism. I feel that in a country where private enterprise and public ownership have done so much for the public welfare we should not discriminate in favour of one or the other; after all they are only agencies. Whether a service is performed by one or the other of these instruments which the nation in the past has used to such great advantage should not concern us so much as whether the action performed is done properly and to the greatest degree will promote the common good. To private enterprise we owe the discovery, the colonization and the early development of this great Dominion, and to private enterprise we owe most of ihe prosperity that we enjoy. Yes, Sir, private enterprise has done so much for the welfare of Canada and is still operating so beneficially, that we cannot turn our backs upon it. It deserves better treatment than scorn, contempt and ingratitude; and if before the committee, to which I hope this bill will be referred, it is found that the Montreal, Ottawa and Georgian Bay Canal Company can carry out the great project of constructing the canal and developing electrical energy, I cannot see

Georgian Bay Can .1 Company
that I could object to the measure for the reason that what is proposed is not a public enterprise.
Let U3 amend the charter, if necessary, in order to protect the rights of all concerned; but let us not delay or thwart the execution of a plan which means so much for the future of this country. In our vote on this question, let us consider not so much the question of the oharter itself, let us consider not simply the principle of public ownership or the interests of the National Hydro or any other concern, let us not consider even the canal itself, but let us stand for the country that we love and cherish and whose interests we place above all other considerations.
In my opinion the stand we should take, in order to maintain our reputation as serious men, is the stand that was adopted, by the hem. member for Lisgar. If we do that I am satisfied that we shall secure the end we have in view: that our great natural resources shall be preserved and developed in such a way as to secure the maximum of benefit for the great mass of the common people of Canada. Let us look to the committee to whom this project may be entrusted to consider the question in that light, and to make a careful and impartial study of the great problem of national transportation.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
In rising to continue the debate on this question, which has been discussed until the subject has almost been worn threadbare, let me say that I have no apologies to offer. I consider what is proposed here one of the greatest steals ever attempted in the twentieth century and when I say that I do not forget the things that have been put over the people of this country in the past.
After the very able speeches that have been made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Guthrie), the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett), and the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland), it is very hard indeed, as I am sure hon. members generally will agree, to find something new or interesting to say on this subject. Nevertheless, in the few remarks that I shall make I shall endeavour to avoid as far as possible rehashing any of the statements and excuses put forward by previous speakers, except to the extent necessary to preserve the continuity of my argument.
If I had my way I would not only wipe out the charter we are considering but every charter on the Ottawa river, and leave the Ottawa river and the power thereon free as it ought to be to the people of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. I approach the consideration of this subject, and the question of the power development that is involved from the standpoint of what will contribute most to the upbuilding of the country. I feel that the development of power is as inevitably connected with the development of our country as in our timber, our minerals, our pulpwood, or any other of our natural resources. I look forward to the time when this Dominion will have a great increase of population, and when the provinces of Ontario and Quebec will be peopled by from ,<velve to fifteen millions of souls. I look forward with much interest to the development of the province from which I come and I wish to preserve to the public, rather than alienate to private interests, not only the water-powers located on this river but those existing on the other streams of Canada.
The charter, the renewal of which we are considering, has been in existence for something over thirty years and those who hold it have failed to live up to its terms. Otherwise that charter would not be before us today for renewal. We have to consider that renewal not only in the light of past events but in the light of to-day, bearing in mind the great increase in the value of electrical energy which has come about within recent years, and the enormous demand for it. I am one of those who believe it is the duty of the government and of parliament to preserve these great heritages of the past and to administer them as a trust for the benefit of the people. To me it seems strange that the government who are in power at the present time, although this bill has been before this House for the twelfth time, have had practically nothing to say on such an important issue.
I want to refer very briefly to the remarks of the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Chevrier) who introduced this bill. I have been wondering whether the promoters have been quite frank with parliament in regard to this project or whether their contempt for the intelligence of parliament is so great they thought they could, in the vernacular of the street, "put one over" the members of the House of Commons. This is what the hon. member for Ottawa said, as reported on page 1387 of Hansard:
I come now to the question asked me a moment ago: Is this a canal charter or is its object the development of power? Well, no matter how the question may be argued; no matter what is said, I affirm that under the terms of the charter which the promoters of this bill are endeavouring to have renewed, nothing is contemplated but the construction of the canal.
Was the hon. member for Ottawa frank with this House or was he not? If he was frank

Georgian Bay Canal Company
with this House, was he frank with the company which he is supposed to represent in this House, because looking at the last paragraph of the bill I find that the promoters are asking for a renewal not only of their charter for the construction of a canal, but of the power rights which were slipped into this charter many years after it was originally granted? If they are asking only for the right to construct a canal, why is he asking to have confirmed in the present bill the power rights which were slipped in there in 1912? If they are asking for the power rights, why does he stand before parliament and solemnly declare that all the company wants is the privilege of constructing a canal? Furthermore, in the last clause it is provided that if certain conditions are not fulfilled the canal rights lapse, but there is not a similar provision in regard to the power rights. Therefore I say again to the hon. member for Ottawa that it appears to me that he has not been quite frank either with the House or with the company.
Let us look at his proposition as a canal scheme. The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) was good enough to allow me to read the brief which was placed in his hands by the hon. member for Ottawa. In that brief I find that the estimated cost of this canal was $282,000,000. If we take it for granted that money is worth 5 per cent, the interest on that amount would be something over $14,100,000 per annum. Does he think any canal that had to pay yearly such a vast sum as $14,100,000 interest on the investment, could be made to pay as a canal project? I am quite positive there is not in the world a financial firm that would finance this project simply as a canal. What does that mean? It means that if we assume there would be a saving of three cents a bushel on wheat from the west, as is claimed, the freight rate would still be six cents a bushel, and that would involve, in order to pay the interest on the investment, bringing over this canal something like 235.000,000 bushels a year. Was ever a more absurd proposition put before a body of intelligent people? In addition to this we must remember that this canal would have to do business in competition with the other free canals of the Dominion of Canada. Therefore, looked at from a business standpoint, the thing is absurd.
Further, I find from the brief which the hon. member for Bow River kindly placed in my hands, that the company have no intention simply of building a canal system. They grant, as has been granted by everybody, that the navigable waters are under the control of the Dominion, but they make the express

declaration that there are no surplus waters on the Ottawa river and that all those waters will be under their control as they will own the dams, control the sluiceways, and thus control the time and place at which the water is let out. Consequently they will be absolutely in control of the water-powers on the Ottawa river.
That brings us right up against the great proposition of provincial rights which has been fought out in the past in this country. I am surprised, when I look across this chamber, to see a government sitting here, called a Liberal government, when from the beginning of this debate to the present time, not a single member has risen in his place to defend the principle of provincial rights. My mind goes back in history to the days of Sir Oliver Mowat, the Hon. Edward Blake, and the great battles that were fought in those days by the Liberal party for provincial rights in this country. I say to myself: How are the mighty fallen! To-day there is not on the Liberal side a voice that can be raised on behalf of the provincial rights of this country. They sit there wedded to the big interests of Canada, helpless, and they have nothing to say on behalf of that policy which was one of the big factors in creating the great Liberal party of the past.
I would like, for example;, to ask the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) if he remembers the chorus of the Liberal campaign song of some thirty or forty years ago, a song written by the wife of a cabinet minister, the Hon. J. D. Edgar, whose painting we see out in the hall. It went something like this:
The traitor's hand is on thy throat, Ontario, Ontario,
Suppress the traitor with thy vote, Ontario, Ontario.
That was the campaign song of the Liberal party thirty or forty years ago. Where does that party stand to-day? Where are these great upholders of provincial rights in this country? I would like to ask the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) where he stands on this question. Is he standing up for the knight that formerly represented his constituency, or is he standing for the interests of the common people that he and his party love so well to talk about? Might I remind him in passing that the Conservative party of the province of Ontario, provineially speaking, is to-day endeavouring to carry hydroelectric energy to every farm in this country? They have spent millions already. They have built something like 1,800 miles of primary and secondary power lines, to carry that power to the farmers of this country. Is he going

Georgian Bay Canal Company
to stand up for the farmer who will have the power on his farm to grind his corn, to saw his wood, to light his barn, or for the housewife to churn her butter? Or is he going to stand up for the plutocrat and the big interests which are seeking to grab a million or a million and a quarter horse-power on the Ottawa river? When the farmers of this country and all the industrial interests of eastern Ontario needed that power so badly the Ontario Hydro Electric Power Commission had to go over into the province of Quebec to buy some 266,000 horse-power from the Gatineau in order to supply the wants of eastern Ontario. They have been blocked for years in their efforts to extend the great hydro of western Ontario in the east because of these big interests' that were attempting to control the franchise on the Ottawa. Is he going to pass by the poor farmer and the workingman, and take his seat beside Dives at the rich man's table?
Where is the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) ? He gave us an interesting discourse a while ago. He said: "I do not believe anybody can frame an amendment that will make the bill suitable, but I am willing to pass it on to committee in the hope I suppose that the promoters or somebody behind them may supply the brains to do it." Might I remind the House, Mr. Speaker, that a few months ago Mr. Harry Sifton gave an interview in Toronto. In that interview he told the press that the Liberal party had the halters on nearly all the Progressives of this country. As I look across the House and see Liberals to the front of them, Liberals behind them, Liberals to the left of them and Liberals to the right of them, I wonder if he was not speaking the truth. When I see men like the hon. member for Lisgar get up, because Harry Sifton cracks the whip, as he has done over the present parliament, when I see him using all the force he can to pull a $100,000,000 contract from the people of this country safely within the grasp of the big interests of Canada, I wonder what we are coming to in this country. Where is the great Progressive party that a few years ago shouted to the heavens for the interests of the common people? Have they departed or have they not? Well, we will soon know. When this vote takes place we will know whether Mr. Sifton has the halter upon these people or whether he has not. The people of Canada to-day are looking to this House, and thejr will look at the vote that is to be taken to-night, and to-morrow they will size up the situation and will know whether Mr. Sifton was right or whether he was wrong.
For a moment, let me visualize this graft, if I may. Let me bring before this House and the country the magnitude of it, in order that they may better know what they are voting on to-night. It just so happens, Sir, that I can very easily do this, because in the province of Ontario we have the Hydro Electric Power Commission which has developed electrical energy to the extent of something over 960,000 horse-power, not as great as this development will be, but something in the neighbourhood of three-quarters of it, and when I tell hon. members what that commission has done they will see the possibilities that lie before the people who obtain the franchise or the power rights on the Ottawa river, if they do obtain them. We have in the province of Ontario to-day, 410 municipalities using electrical power that was developed by the Hydro Electric Power Commission of Ontario. There are 402,000 consumers. We have over 5,000 miles of transmission line with a generating ^capacity of 961,000 horse-power, and they have invested $276,000,000 in capital. They would have done more, Sir, had they not been retarded in the eastern end of the province and had not the whole provincial development been held up by such companies as are seeking today to renew this franchise. What has that meant to the people of Ontario? The cost of the power delivered to the doors of the people to-day is less than one-quarter of what it was before the hydroelectric came into existence. Let us visualize that and put it into dollars and cents, and we find that the saving to the people of the province of Ontario in 1925 was something over $36,000,000, comparing hydro with pre-hydro rates. Does that mean anything to the people of this country, or does it not? Does that tell the House and the country the possibilities that lie behind the franchise for the power on the Ottawa river-$36,000,000 saved to the people of Ontario in one year? They pay that much less than they would have had to pay under pre-hydro rates.
Let me give another comparison.' It was stated in this House the other day that the rates under private ownership were lower than the rates under public ownership, as ex-emplied in the Hydro Electric Power Commission. I have in my hand a comparison which deals first with domestic lighting and heating. I will take the cities of Toronto, Hamilton, London and Montreal, three of them under hydro, and one under private ownership, and then I will go to the United States and take Buffalo and Detroit. I find

Georgian Bay Canal Company
that for domestic lighting and cooking for the same quantity in each case, Toronto is paying $45.97, Hamilton and London the same, Montreal $76.87, Buffalo $174.20 and Detroit $124.38. Then for commercial lighting, which is a little bit different, Toronto is paying $357.60, Hamilton $140.48, London $228.50, 'Montreal $1,147.70, Buffalo $811.70 and Detroit $936.17.
I will not bother the House with the figures for power, because it is hardly germane to this matter, but the proportion is pretty much the same, showing that the preservation of this power for the use of the people is one of the great functions of parliament to-day.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I was a little confused at the start about the mystery surrounding this subject. We were told during the course of the debate that behind the bill was a mystery company. Some said it was Sir Clifford Sifton and his confreres, while others declared he had nothing to do with it. I do not know who is behind the bill, and I cannot say that I care. During the past week I have devoted considerable time to ^reading musty volumes of Hansard containing the debates between 1900 and 1907, and I was startled at the great mystery which surrounded the doings of the government at that time just as we see a similar mystery surrounding the present government. I found, for example, that there was then in existence a mystery company called the North Atlantic Trading Company. It seemed like the world at its creation-it was without form and void. But it had one distinguishing characteristic, an insatiable capacity for swallowing money. It was supposed to have its headquarters at Amsterdam, but no one there knew anything about it, for it apparently was not a corporate entity. With this mystery company the government of the day entered into an agreement under which the company were to get five dollars, or one pound sterling, for every man, woman and child that it brought into Canada. AVhere the immigrants came from did not matter; with the exception of the citizens of a few countries, everyone was welcome. And it did not matter whether they stayed here or not, once they were brought to this country the company was entitled to payment. I continued my research and I found that something mysterious happened in connection with half-breed scrip. An order in council was passed making it lawful to purchase this scrip from holders outside the Dominion, and in some mysterious way that order in council was suppressed for three months. During that period agents from Winnipeg used their time to good purpose and bought up some 30,000 to 35,000 acres of land covered by this scrip, for which they paid at the rate of from one to two hundred dollars for 240 acres of land. A mystery? Do hon. members see any similarity between the present mystery and the mysteries of those days?
I pursued my investigations a little further and found a mystery connected with Saskatchewan, called the Saskatchewan Land Company, to which 250,000 acres of land in that province, supposed to be desert, was sold for a dollar an acre. But strange to say, within two years afterwards it proved to be a very fertile rose garden. Another mystery? Why, of course, whoever heard of cold-blooded business men buying up 250,000 acres of desert land? I found also another company, this time in the Peace river territory, called the Peace River Colonization Company, to which was transferred 336,000 acres of land for a dollar an acre-twenty-five cents down, twenty-five cents in five years, and the balance in ten. I found further that extensive lands had been leased out there, and that nine of the leases were so drawn that they could not be revoked I have the names and the figures here, but I will not weary the House with them. I will not weary the House with a recital of the other mysteries that I unearthed, such as the timber limits, Yukon liquor permits, et cetera. My only reason for bringing these mysteries of the past to the attention of hon. members is that we have to-day a mystery company behind which are certain mysterious individuals whom nobody seems to know. I ask the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) if he is credulous enough to believe that-

I have
listened these many weeks with more or less patience, or impatience, to the arguments advanced on both sides of this controversy and I have tried to separate the wheat from the chaff, the relevant from the irrelevant, to discover what the real issue is. What is the question that is before the House to-day? What is the question we shall decide by our votes if we vote to-day? The question is not, shall we or shall we not have the Georgian bay canal? It is not, shall we or shall we not develop water-powers on the Ottawa river? It is not, shall we or shall we not have public ownership in this country? The immediate question which we shall decide by our votes is, shall we or shall we not send this bill to the committee to be investigated? That is the issue in the impending vote.
Much has been said during this debate about the principle involved. I ask, what is the principle involved? It is not the great principle of public ownership, neither is it the wicked principle of private enterprise. Ii is not the great principle of provincial rights, neither is it the principle of federal jurisdiction; for the question is, shall we refer this bill to the committee? Shall we investigate it and see what is in it? It is not even a question of the high and lofty principles of Sir Herbert Holt as opposed to the wicked principles of Sir Clifford Sifton; the question is, shall we investigate this bill and see what it proposes? The real principle which is at stake is this: shall this parliament maintain its ancient right to investigate, before its own committees, questions of great public importance? That is the issue in a nutshell. That is what we shall decide by our vote on this amendment.
Let me review for a moment the history of this project. The charter was issued for the canal away back in 1894. Those who secured the charter were to build the canal, and in exchange they were to have the water-powers. They could not secure the money to dig the cana'l. Why? speechtext:
Ontario and

A very interesting question was raised by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) in regard to the right of this country to have that canal built at the expense of the people living along its banks. He argued that if you make the power pay for the building of the canal you make the people who live near the canal pay for their power, while the surplus would be used to build' a canal for the benefit of people in a remote part of the Dominion, or for the Dominion as a whole. Mr
Speaker, I do not intend to depart from my customarj' practice of seldom and then only briefly addressing .this House, but I cannot record my vote upon the question now before the House without giving some of the reasons why I intend to support the amendment. The subject has been exhaustively discussed. The logical and forceful speech of the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) and the convincing eloquence and close scrutiny of the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) leave practically nothing to be said. I must confess that I was astonished a moment ago at the statement made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell), namely; "If we can get a canal for nothing, why should we not accept it?" He put that question as if he had considered that it terminated the whole discussion. I ask the Minister of Agriculture if in all this country there is a single canal, large or small, from the Newmarket canal in North York

Georgian Bay Canal Company
to the Welland canal, that has been acquired for nothing. There is not one, nor will there ever be a canal built in Canada for nothing. The taxpayers pay for every canal that we have. Therefore I take it that the Minister of Agriculture, in his usual good-natured and facetious manner, did not mean his remark to be taken seriously.
The question resolves itself into two parts: the transportation or canal part and the water-power part. In respect of the canal I say with full assurance that there is not an hon. member sitting in this House, there is not a reading man in all Canada outside of an insane asylum, and I should not think there would be many within the walls of such an institution, who believe that the money to build this canal, considered solely as a transportation system, can be obtained in any financial centre in the world. I recall well some thirty-three years ago when the charter was originally granted, when estimates were made as to the cost of the undertaking, and at that time the cost was placed at approximately S100,000,000. If $100,000,000 were required thirty-three years ago to construct a twenty or twenty-two foot waterway from Georgian bay to Montreal, I submit to the knowledge and intelligence of memhers that it will require at least two and one-half times that amount to do the same work to-day. That is not an exaggerated estimate, and so we arrive, moderately, conservatively, at a sum of $250,000,000 as requisite to build a system of navigation known as the Georgian bay canal capable of passing vessels with a draft of twenty feet or as they are sometimes termed, 10.000 ton vessels, the largest that navigate lake Superior and the other upper lakes.
First of all, even though the bonds were backed by the Dominion of Canada that money would cost close upon 5 per cent. Over and above that you have the cost of operating and the cost of repairs and maintenance. Therefore, figure it out as you will, you cannot arrive at a lower sum than S15.000.000 a year in connection with this project. What sane financier, what sane person is going to put a dollar into an enterprise from which not one cent of revenue is to be derived? Let it be remembered that I am speaking of the transportation scheme and not at the moment of the water-power end of.it.
The promoters of this bill profess that they will complete this waterway to a depth capable of floating vessels of 10,000 tons. Where in the name of common sense are they going to get the money? The thing upon its face is absurd; it is too nonsensical for any serious
man to mention for a moment. It will take $15,000,000 a year to carry the cost of this canal if it' is built as professed by the promoters of the bill. In a circular which has been addressed to every member of this House the statement is made that by this proposed waterway there will be a saving of three cents a bushel in the cost of freighting from Fort William to the port of Montreal. Upon the basis of the largest quantity of not simply wheat, but grain, namely 295,000,000 bushels, that has come out of lake Superior ports-and I hope in the future that figure will be greatly exceeded-this saving of three cents a bushel will represent a little less than $9,000,000. Why, it would pay the taxpayers of Canada well-it would be money in their pockets-if they gave a subsidy of three cents a bushel to the farmers of the northwest for every bushel of grain they exported in the big crop year of 1925-26, because instead of the taxpayers of this country paying $15,000,000 a year to maintain the waterway, including of course interest on the cost, they would have to pay only $9,000,000 on a basis of an economy of three cents a bushel.
This is a point which has always appealed to me in connection with this question. After due consideration many years ago the Dominion government and the parliament of Canada concluded that the best waterway from lake Superior, lake Huron and the other upper lakes to the sea was by the Welland canal to the St. Lawrence river, or what is popularly known as the St. Lawrence waterway. We have invested already upwards of $60,000,000, I think, in the Welland canal, and it is not at all unlikely that before the enlarged canal is completed the cost will run to $75,000,000. The proposal is to have the transhipping go through in smaller vessels which can pass through the St. Lawrence canal, but I would think that ultimately, as soon as the finances of the country permit, the sensible, businesslike project would be to enlarge the St. Lawrence, so as to permit the largest of the upper lake freighters to pass right down to the port of Montreal, or, if you like, the port of Quebec, where transhipment would take place. Are we to enter deliberately, with our eyes open, into competition, by means of this Georgian bay canal, with the St. Lawrence waterways, in which we have already invested a great' many million dollars, and in which every day of the year we are burying more and more money? A few years ago, in a fit of frenzied finance, the government and the parliament of this country

and I am bound to say with the approval of the electors-built three transcontinental railways where two at most would

have sufficed. There is no one, I venture to say, who to-day does not regard that policy as a fatuous one, as an uneconomical one. We know that a good deal of the burden of taxation under whidh this country labours arises out of that extravagant railway policy of a few years ago, and yet hon. members stand up in this House and ask us to pursue the same fatuous policy in connection with water transportation and to build two canal systems where one is adequate.
Assuming, merely for the purpose of argument, that the Georgian bay canal project will be completed in the course of years, every bushel of grain that passes down it will be taken from the other waterway, the St. Lawrence, which we are completing at very great cost. The total revenue of all canals of Canada is less than $1,000,000, and of that $900,000 two-thirds are derived from elevating charges on the Welland canal and from some water leases on the Lachine canal. But I am glad to say that there is not one dollar of tolls upon our canals, and yet the promoters of this bill say to us that they will spend $250,000,000 upon the project without the imposition of one single dollar of tolls from which they can derive one penny of revenue. Sir, it seems to me that the project, as a canal, ought literally to be laughed out of the House.
Then we come to the other aspect, namely, the waterways. My attitude-I speak only for myself-in respect to water-power is that the matter should be left entirely to the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. My understanding is that under a not very remote judgment of the Privy Council it was decided that the riverbeds and the shores belonged' to the province, and without a dissenting voice the legislature of. Ontario, although overwhelmingly Conservative in its party complexion, and the legislature of Quebec, equally overwhelmingly Liberal in its complexion, unanimously passed resolutions condemning this bill and asking parliament to throw it out. Surely those resolutions ought to receive some consideration in this House. I recall well many years ago, and the hon. member for Muskolca (Mr. McGibbon) alluded to it in his address, when, misguidedly, a Conservative government, prompted by the request of one of their supporters, namely, the late Dalton McCarthy entered into a controversy with the province of Ontario over many serious questions such for instance as the Streams Bill, another relating to the licensing for the sale of intoxicating liquors, and other matters. In every instance the Dominion government was beaten, and the Conservative party lost caste in that provfMr. White.]
ince for many years because of its attitude towards the provincial government of Ontario. I warn the government, whether this bill goes to second reading or not, that if it cracks the party whip and induces members to vote on account of party allegiance for the second reading, it will be digging its own grave as sure as death and taxation.
There is another aspect of this question which in my judgment has not been adequately stressed, and it is the danger of getting into litigation over these waterways. At this moment the holders of the charter, popularly known as the Sifton interests, have not one single copper of vested rights. They acquired this charter, so the story runs, for speculative purposes and for none other. The charter expires on the 1st of May next, a matter of four weeks and a few days, and if the charter is allowed to expire the gentlemen who entered into this speculation will be out a few dollars. Dealing with the matter of vested rights, these people have had this charter for thirty-three years, and can any hon. member tell me where a single sod has been turned towards the construction of the work? The story goes-and I do not vouch for it, but I would not be surprised if there were some truth in it, knowing the moderation of the gentlemen who hold this charter- that they are willing to relinquish it for a recompense of $2,000,000. I admire their moderation! I wish I possessed even a modicum of it. But if we put this bill into committee, and if we report it back from committee-emasculated if you like, not even a skeleton, a bare shadow of the bill as it had been in the past-we will in a measure have confirmed certain rights to these interests. I am against such a course. Litigation will follow. No one knows it better than the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). The provinces of Ontario and Quebec have already stated in the most unequivocal language that they will have recourse to the courts. If you give the promoters any kind of standing room, they will make it so difficult to move along the lines of the development of power that the whole project will be held up for an indefinite time.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the members of the government have expressed no opinion upon the merits or demerits of this bill. What may be in their minds I of course, not being a Stuart Cumberland, cannot tell; but if their intent be to so emasculate the measure in committee that it will become innocuous and absolutely harmless, it seems to me that it is upon the principle of the prevention of cruelty to animals-that in order to make the

Georgian Bay Canal Company
operation less painful they should take an inch at a time off the dog's tail. As we all know, this is not an ordinary private bill. It would be better described as a public bill in the hands of a private member.
The hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young) told us this afternoon that he has had difficulty in making up his mind. He wants more information, he wants experts called and the matter gone into fully before the committee within-as we all hope-two weeks from prorogation. But if he has any doubt as to the meaning of the bill, I think he stands alone in this House and in the country, for its merits or demerits have been discussed on platforms and in the press ad nauseam, and there is no one so dull, no one so blind or stupid, as not to be aware that this is a fight by the promoters for power rights, and that it is not for one moment to be taken seriously as a transportation project.
Of course, we can all understand and sympathize sincerely with the position of the Prime Minister. There are such things, I suppose, as political debts. There is sometimes political work which must be paid for. I would not be surprised in the least if the desire of the first minister to send this bill to a committee is a payment on account, as it were, for services rendered by one of the promoters in an effort to avenge the defeat which in 1925 the Prime Minister sustained in North York. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not any intention of speaking on this bill, but as I championed it in past sessions I deem it necessary to express my views on this occasion. I well remember making a speech favouring the Georgian bay canal, and the late lamented Emmanuel B. Devlin, the member for Wright, afterwards said in my hearing, although he did not know I was within range of his voice, "Baldwin has knocked the props from under my feet."
I speak in favour of the Georgian bay canal as I would of any other great waterway for the development of this country, for I believe this is the cheapest kind of transportation. A member on the other side of the House last week gave us an historical resume of canals back even before the birth of Christ and told us all about the waterways of China and thus down through history to comparatively modern times, showing that he had at least studied this method of transportation. Today we find canals are not paying propositions. I notice quite recently that the Erie canal is not doing as much business as the old canal did. When I spoke of the Georgian bay canal project on former occasions there was not then any real appreciation of the wonderful assets we had in the hinterland of Quebec and Ontario. We had pretty much the same railway facilities then as we have to-day, but there was not the same necessity as now exists for the construction of a canal such as this. In the interior of Quebec and Ontario there is a wonderful mineral country and just now large sums are being spent in the production of gold, of which considerable quantities have already been found. It is intended to delve still deeper into the earth in search of this and other precious metals, and with iron ore, which the geologists believe to exist in that part of the country, together with copper, silver and other assets which undoubtedly are waiting tc be taken, there are great prospects ahead of these provinces. I do not think that the country there could be better or more cheaply served in the way of transportation than by

Georgian Bay Canal Company
means of such a waterway as is proposed. Our mineral products in these sections of Quebec and Ontario, of which I am speaking, would afford enormous traffic even though so far only the fringe of that country has been touched.
This question involves a conflict between private and public ownership. In my opinion, which differs from the view advanced by my hon. friend from Mount Royal (Mr. White), if the hydro-electric posibilities are such as have been depicted, this great wealth should contribute to the cost of constructing the canal. I believe that it could be so arranged as to have the revenue from this hydro-electric development pay in time, if not immediately, for the Georgian bay canal. If it comes to a question of American versus Canadian interests I would1 not hesitate to favour the development of this power by our own people. Someone has said that this is a matter of Montreal or the Holt interests as against Toronto and the Sifton interests. However that may be, I would have no hesitation in any instance in advocating that Canadians be allowed to develop this power rather than hand it over to American interests who, I am sure, would have but one purpose in view, namely, the exportation of power to the United States, making us hewers of wood and drawers of water to their own advantage. That I would oppose on every occasion. If hydroelectric power is to be developed an enormous amount of labour and capital will be required. Let us keep these in Canada; let it never be said that transmission lines in connection with the development of power along this route were constructed by outsiders for the benefit of foreign labour. Let us see to it that our great heritage of white coal, of which we have more probably than exists in any other country, we have been able'to take advantage of and to exploit ourselves.
We are prone to speak of the vastness of this country, but I think I am within the mark when I say there is a possibility of our developing 20,000,000 horse-power in this country. This is one of the most glorious visions before Canadians to-day. I firmly believe that if the Georgian bay canal is built noiw, or at any time in the future, it should be built with the great water-power possibilities in view. I do not urge any haste in such a stupendous undertaking as this. In my own private affairs I have never robbed the future for the sake of the present. I believe in conservation. I believe in conserving all our resources, whether they be timber, our fisheries or our minerals, and not in being greedy and thinking only of ourselves. Let us think of posterity.

This question cannot be decided without the most careful consideration. There is a. multitude of complex considerations that must be weighed:	provincial and riparian rights,
federal rights, and all the rest of it-matters which this parliament cannot deal with without a thorough investigation. I believe the people are intelligent enough not to do anything that will divide province against province or the provinces against the Dominion. Let us do nothing that will result in litigation. I have confidence enough in the good sense of our people to believe that nothing of this sort will happen. It seems' to me that the best way in which this whole question can be handled is to have the bill referred to the committee where it could be fully discussed.
We have heard a good deal about this charter hanging fire for thirty-three years. What are the reasons why no progress has been made towards the construction of the canal? The great, appalling war came along, and are we not proud of Canada to-day to see that her finances are in such good condition after that great struggle? Not only did the war interfere but the construction of the Welland canal was undertaken, and those who have seen that canal will know that it is a most ponderous undertaking; in the course of that construction it has been found necessary to dig through great banks of clay which have no solid foundation, entailing an enormous amount of work. I say without hesitation that I believe the Georgian bay canal should have been built first, which would have promoted the development of the tremendous resources of those portions of Quebec and Ontario in that vicinity; I believe a greater benefit would have been obtained to this country if the Welland canal had been allowed to wait until the construction of the Georgian bay canal had been finished. Some'hon. members representing constituencies bordering the great lakes may not agree with that, but I maintain that the Georgian bay canal would have been a greater asset to the trade and commerce of this country and would have hastened the development of our great natural resources.
I do not care to elaborate upon this matter, but I am emphatically in favour of this bill being sent to committee where those who are backing it may appear and make known their promises and pledges in this connection. I would not allow the great hydro-electric possibilities of this country to be destroyed without, first making certain that this canal will be built. I am not enough of an engineer even to approximate the cost of this undertaking, but I believe this canal should be built piece by piece, beginning at the Ottawa end if you will and gradually extending it until

Georgian Bay Canal Company
it is completed. Not one horse-power of hydro-electric energy should be sacrificed or given away to anyone, whether they be Canadian or foreign, until a binding agreement has been made between the province of Quebec, the province of Ontario and the federal government. These three governments should work in conjunction and in perfect unanimity, under an agreement which will be binding upon each for all time, in order that this may be a source of great national development and an undertaking of which all Canada may be proud.
Mr. R. E. RYERjSON (Brantford City): Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to take up more than a few moments of the time of the House on this question, but representing as I do an industrial centre which has enjoyed for many years the full benefits of the hydro-electric system of Ontario, I deem it my duty to protest against the granting of a renewal of this charter and against any measure which may appear to menace the future of this great public-owned enterprise.
For the purpose of a better understanding of the attitude of the people of Ontario, and particularly those served by hydro in their relation to this question, I would like to state a few facts pertaining to the early h:story and present status of this project. The Ontario Hydro Electric system did not originate with the Ontario government or with any one individual, as has been frequently stated on the floor of thin House. The entire plan was carried out and now stands as a partnership affair between the government of Ontario and the municipalities served by the system, both as to construction and financial obligation. The government is responsible for the purchasing, development and transmission of electrical energy to the gates of the municipalities which, on their part, take care of the construction and maintenance of distribution plants and stepping-down stations. A small league of municipalities comprising the cities and towns of Toronto, London, Brantford, Guelph, Stratford, Woodstock and Ingersoll were the initial pioneers in advocating and planning this great development.
The early efforts of this league were directed towards the preservation, development and public ownership of the vast potential power at Niagara Falls, which was rapidly being sacrificed and given away to large private interests, greatly to the advantage of American industry and American citizens. This pioneer work, which included surveys, engineers'' reports and a general campaign of publicity, was carried on for a number of years. In 1903, at the request of these municipalities, the Ontario government of that date passed an act authorizing the creation of the Ontario Power Commission, with power to investigate the feasibility of the development and transmission of Niagara power to points in central and southern Ontario, and to prepare plans for such a purpose. The personnel of the commission was named by the league of municipalities, and the entire cost was borne by that league. Those nominated to the commission were:
E. W. B. Snyder, St. Jacobs, president.
P. W. Ellis, Toronto.
W. F. Cockshutt, Brantford. _
Adam Beck, London.
R. F. Fessenden, electrical engineer, Washington, D.C.
Before the final report of this commission was completed a number of other municipalities joined the league, including Hamilton, Dundas, Paris, St. Thomas, St. Marys, Mitchell, Kitchener, Waterloo, Hespeler, Preston and Galt. After the completion of this report and at the request of this now influential league of municipalities-and with the persuasive powers of Adam Beck-the then government under the leadership of Sir James Whitney adopted the plans and took over the project. The Ontario Hydro Electric Commission was created, under whose management and supervision the original plans were developed and extended into the present system, which has saved millions of dollars to the consumers of power in this province. The people of these municipalities have watched with a justifiable pride the wonderful success and growth of hydro, and naturally look with alarm and suspicion on any action by this parliament which would appear to interfere with or jeopardize the future success of this great public undertaking.
I not only voice my own disapproval of this bill, but desire as well to add the protest of the city of Brantford, which unanimously passed the following resolution:
That the council of the municipality of Brantford respectfully urges the parliament of Canada not to renew the charter of the Montreal, Ottawa and Georgian Bay Canal Company, known as Bill No. 78, as in our opinion this bill is not in the interest of the province of Ontario as it is an attempt to deprive the people of this province of their right to the powers to be developed from the waters of the Ottawa river, and further that this charter has been in existence for thirty-three years, and no actual construction has taken place, and we believe the renewal of this charter would be contrary and prejudicial to the public interest.
I also have a communication from the town council of the town of Paris, enclosing a similar resolution, which reads as follows:

Georgian Bay Canal Company
That the council of the municipality of Paris, Ontario, respectfully urges the parliament of Canada not to renew the charter of the Montreal, Ottawa and Georgian Bay Canal ComPany, known as Bill No. 78, as in our opinion this bill is not in the interest of the province of Ontario as it is an attempt to deprive the people of this province of their right to the powers to be developed from the water of the Ottawa river, and further that this charter has been in existence for thirty-three years and no actual construction has taken place, and we believe the renewal would be contrary and prejudicial to the public interest.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have been an interested spectator during this debate which has now lasted for some three weeks, and I have at times wondered why there is this wide divergence of views on the question which is now before the House. As I look across the way at the members representing the United Farmers of Alberta., also my good Labour members and other members on the other side who in the most trenchant language condemn those who would send this bill to committee, I think I can assure them-and I would preface my remarks by saying that honesty and sincerity is written all over their countenances-that with all their professions they are not more true nor more loyal to the principle of public ownership than are those who would treat this bill as all other similar bills are treated, namely, by sending it to committee. Oh, yes, but someone says, when we vote on the second reading, when we submit the measure to committee, we are committed to' the principle of it. I am inclined to think that theory was rather badly shot in 1925 when the Petersen contract was before the House. We all recall very well that long drawn out debate, and members on the opposite side of the House who were opposing that measure going to committee declared that we were admitting the principle of subsidies to steamship companies or the principle of subsidies itself.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext: There was a marked distinction. That was a public government measure, not a regular private measure, and it went to a special committee for consideration.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext: That is a stronger reason why this, being a private bill, should go to committee.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext: I would like to remind my hon. friend that on that particular memorable occasion to which he refers, the Prime Minister notified the House that, -notwithstanding all that he said, a vote on that occasion would not be considered as a vote for the principle of the Petersen contract.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
Quite so, and there and then we established the precedent. I think it was taken for granted upon that occasion that we were not committed in any way to the principle of the measure, and I am sure there are a large number of hon. members who may vote to send this bill to committee, who do not consider that they are thereby committing themselves on the question of public versus private ownership.
I was not surprised at the course which our Conservative friends followed. It was a very characteristic one; they took that same natural Conservative attitude, smug, selfrighteous, that they are the only people who are defending the rights of the masses. I think I can assure them also -that there are in this House others who are just as anxious, just as determined as are my good friends the Conservatives, to promote the interests of the great mass of the people. The Conservative party, at least up to the present, have never been conspicuous in respect to the rights of that great mass of the people known as the taxpayers of this country, and particularly in respect to public ownership.
We have, however, in this particular question one feature that, is unique in the economic life of this Dominion, if not of the American continent, in that the river in question, the Ottawa, which has been recognized for at least a hundred years as a navigable waterway, forms an interprovincial boundary. I db not presume to be an authority on constitutional matters, but according to our constitution the water of this stream belongs to the people of Canada. The river bed, as the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) told us the other night, belongs to the provinces, and therefore he contended-and I think it was an ingenious argument-that this set up an (insurmountable problem. Let me tell him that there is no problem at all because, while it may be true that the river bed belongs to the provinces, the Dominion has the right of expropriation at any time and can expropriate for any purposes which it sees fit.
But this constitutes an added reason why this whole question should1 go 'before the committee. We have, as I have said, a stream of which the water belongs to the Dominion and the potential powers belong to the provinces.

Georgian Bay Canal Company
On one side of the Ottawa river we have a province that is avowedly in favour of private ownership and on the other side a province professing public ownership. I wonder if our friends who are opposing this measure and who are declaring that this project should be developed as a national undertaking, as I quite agree it should be, will tell U3 just how under those circumstances they are going to develop the Ottawa river. We are up a blind alley.
Is that not a fundamental reason why this whole measure should go to committee where we can get some light in order to pass an intelligent judgment upon it?
I would not have taken part in this debate had it not been that I believe the time has arrived-and I am very much surprised that up to date no one in this chamber has suggested it-for the appointment of a federal hydro-electric power commission. In Ontario of course we have the hydro power commission, and someone may say, "Well, why not let the provinces attend to such matters as the controlling of hydro power?" Very true, but it has to be remembered that the three prairie provinces do not own or control their resources, and I am told by competent engineers that there is known to them at the present time something in excess of ten million of potential hydro power in these three prairie provinces. I have been told that there is something in excess of seven million now known in the province of Manitoba alone. We now witness the struggle that is going on, as we are told by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) between two great financial rings to get control of the powers of what is just a stream; for the Ottawa river is only a little stream compared with the Nelson, the Churchill, the Mackenzie and the Yukon rivers. Someone has said that there is &, million and a quarter horse-power involved. I have made some inquiries and I find that these same competent engineers tell us that they will never develop more than 750,000 horse-power on the Ottawa river. Now we have all this struggle, three weeks of the time of parliament, practically every hour which has been allotted to private members for the consideration of private bills and private measures has been given over to this one question, a matter involving 750,000 horse-power, while as I say there is known to the engineers at least ten million horsepower certain to be developed in the three prairie provinces. These natural resources are to-day controlled by the federal parliament, and the experience, Mr. Speaker, of this long range administration of the last two years has not been very satisfactory to western Canada in respect either to power development or to pulpwood and many other resources which I might mention. The time has arrived when it is essential that these powers should be developed in the best interests of the people of Canada; and if my Conservative friends are as desirous as they appear to be-and I think they are-they will support at once the suggestion of a federal hydropower commission which will take charge of every power in Canada, whether it be on the Ottawa, the Nelson, or any other river. It may be of interest to this House to know that a certain group of financiers have already an option on the largest single power site on the Nelson river, known as the White Mud falls.

When the people of Manitoba are forced to stand by and see two foreign financial rings barter with their very birthright-that is the spectacle we have in Manitoba-with the five million of horse-power on the Nelson river, within about six hundred miles of the city of Winnipeg and about the same distance of some of our western cities, is it not patent to us that in the near future we must take drastic steps to control these powers for the people of western Canada, or of all of Canada if you like, rather than continue the policy which we have been following, of dealing them out in parcels to foreign interests, or to financial interests even though they are not foreign.
With the completion of the Hudson Bay railway; with the opening up of such great resources as are to be found on Belcher islands, where, I am given to understand the largest iron ore deposits on the American continent are to be found; with the vast pulpwood resources along the Nelson and Churchill rivers, we can readily see that by long range administration the best results cannot be obtained. I am making no reflection whatever upon our present Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) who is now in charge of these resources, but he has a big job on his hands. His task is far too great to enable him to give proper consideration to the resources of any one province and have them developed as they should be.
Before concluding I desire again to urge upon the government and upon this House the absolute necessity in my judgment of
Georgian Bay Canal Company

constituting in the very near future-as I think this would be an opportune time- a federal hydro power commission. I would not have risen at all were it not that I had hoped that during this debate some member on the front benches of the official opposition, or some member of the government, would have come forward with a suggestion that the time was ripe for the appointment of such a board. Without any doubt, by far the biggest question, economic or social, in the Dominion of Canada to-day is the matter of hydro development. There is no other single feature of our life that reaches into every avenue of our economic development as that of electricity, and as the years go by it will become increasingly important that the development of hydro must be preserved for the benefit of the people and not allowed to get into the hands of any great financial ring.
I am anxious-and I have no hesitation in saying so-to see this bill go to committee. I want to assure the House that I am not interested at all in the fortunes of either the Siftons or others.
