speechtext:
When I was speaking at the opening off this debate I referred to the fact that those interested in this bill, as well as the public generally and the newspapers, were very apt to refer to this matter only in connection with the Carillon canal and the Carillon power. I endeavoured to make it plain at the time that this is only part of tlhe issue before us to-day. I explained that it was an erroneous view and that the bill deals with all the powers on the Ottawa river, of which the Carillon is only one. This afternoon the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young) referred to the matter.
I do not think I should have risen to say anything about it had not the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Dunning)-the only member of the government Who up to this time has spoken on the subject-made a special 
point of the 'Carillon power. His remarks made on March 14, will be found at page 1194 of Hansard. The following is a short extract:
I deem it necessary to give to the House, if possible, some accurate information respecting the history of what I might call, "the bone of contention", because beyond any question that bone of contention is the Carillon power. There ls ri(d a member of the House who is not aware of that fact, nor is there a member who does not know also that the contention for the bone is, at tile present time, not between any public ownership bodies, but between two great private interests.
I disagree entirely with the hon. minister's statement. He might characterize the Carillon as the knuckle, but it is by no means the whole bone. Carillon is in the county of Argenteuil, which I have the honour to represent in this House. One end of the dam to be built at Carillon would be on that side of the river. The people of Carillon are very anxious to see this power developed, and they have waited for its development for thirty years, patiently or impatiently, which ever way you like to put it. I see in his seat the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) who by the courtesy of the electors represented Argenteuil during one parliament, from 1921 to 1925, but notwithstanding all the influence he then	had he	did	nothing	towards	thedevelopment of	this power.	There	arerumours	abroad	as	to who	controls	theGeorgian bay charter. There are also rumours	current	as	to who	controls	the
National Hydro-Electric Company, which has a lease of the Carillon falls from the Department of Railways and Canals. Personally I have no information as to who really controls, but I think I made it abundantly clear on the earlier occasion when I spoke on this bill that I am against the renewal of the Georgian bay charter. As for the lease of the waterpower at Carillon, I may say again for the information of the House "that in 1925 one of the gentlemen most interested in it came to the county and worked against me as strongly as he could in the election. Therefore I am not here to advocate their claims. But we want this power developed, provided always no right is given to export it. True, a great part of the power when developed would be sent to Montreal and other cities, but its development would be sure to lead to industries being established in the locality, and the people there need the power.
I say again, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Railways and Canals is .wrong. Carillon is only one of the many water-powers covered by this bill. In order that every member may realize that that is the fact, I reiterate that

Georgian Bay Canal Company
this charter covers all the powers on the Ottawa river, the Mattawa river and the French river, and that Carillon is only one of those powers, although it is a large one. In other words, the rich prize that the promoters of this bill are seeking is the control of 200 miles of lake and river and rapids with a potential horsepower of a million and a half, as has been stated on several occasions while the bill has been before the House. On the Ottawa river there is a million and a quarter horse-power, and the power on the other two rivers will bring up the total to a million and a half or perhaps two million. That, I claim, is the bone of contention, and I hope hon. members will not allow any argument to becloud the issue on that point,
Now a few words as to the bill itself. Section 1 provides that:
The Montreal, Ottawa and Georgian Bay Canal Company, hereinafter called "the Company'', may commence the construction of its canals, or any of them,-[DOT]	.
or any of them be it noted.
-and expend fifty thousand dollars thereon, on or before the first day of May, one thousand nine and thirty, and may complete the said canals and put them in operation before the first day of May, one thousand nine hundred and thirty-six.
The section concludes:
-and if such construction is not commenced and such expenditure is not so made, or if the said canals are not completed and put in operation within the said periods respectively, the powers granted to the company by parliament shall cease and be null and void as respects so much of the said canals and works as then remains uncompleted.
I draw particular attention of hon. members to these words:
-the powers granted to the company by parliament shall cease and be null and void, as respects so much of the said canals and works as then remains uncompleted.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, would it not be possible for the company under this authority to develop one or more of the water-powers and sell the electric energy without in any way operating a canal? In considering this point I will not refer to Carillon.

speechtext: Since the hon. gentleman has seen fit to ask that question, will he kindly read the last portion of section 1 in the light of section 5 of the act of 1906, which repealed section 43 of the original charter, and then tell this hon. House whether he is still cf the same opinion?

As I said when
speaking before on this subject, my idea is
that the best way to deal with the matter is to let the charter lapse, and have the government take it over under this clause.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend
mean that the government can take the charter over after it has lapsed?

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
That is merely
a matter of verbiage. What I mean to say is, the government should take it over under the powers contained in the section to which he has referred. But that has nothing to do with the point I am trying to make with regard to section 1 of this bill. As I read section 1, it is altogether possible for the company to develop one power on the Ottawa river in the way I shall set forth, without proceeding any further. If hon. gentlemen will listen to me before shaking their heads they will agree with what I am going to say. In considering this point I will not refer to Carillon at all, because that raises the question of rival interests. Let us suppose that this bill should become law and that the charter were renewed under the terms of section 1. Could not the Georgian Bay Canal Company go to Deux Rivieres, 150 miles from Ottawa, and there build a canal and lock, spending $50,000, as they are obliged to do under this section, or even more, which would be in no way connected with the rest of the canal or works? Could not the company then build a dam to develop waterpower, and not to be used for canal purposes'? Would it not be possible for them to develop the water-power at that particular point, having built a canal in that section in order to carry out the specific terms of section 1, and thereafter sell the electricity thus produced, without doing anything further?

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext: Would not the committee stage be the appropriate place to settle that question?

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
Before I conclude I shall have a few words to say about the committee stage of these proceedings. Let me in the meantime develop the point I have in mind regarding the powers conferred by section 1. I am not a lawyer, and I am not affirming that what I have suggested can be done. I am, however, asking this question: Is it not possible under the terms of section 1 for the company, if they see fit, to do as I have outlined? Could they not, by building the canal and lock at that particular point and so complying with the terms of this section, sell all the power thereby developed without completing any of the rest of the waterway? And could they not do that at other points on the Ottawa river?
ids
Georgian Bay Canal Company

If they did, what remedy would there be? All that this parliament could do would be to declare the powers of the company null and void as respects so much of the canals and works as then remained uncompleted. But parliament could not take away the works already built. Thiis section provides that they shall complete and put into operation the whole of the works before the first of May, 1936. But suppose that when that time came nothing had been done except the construction at Deux Rivieres, where by building a high dam and putting the water back twenty miles or so they could develop a large horse-power: what remedy would the country have in that case? None. And the same argument would apply to other rapids and waterfalls on the Ottawa river.
It seems to me that this is a question worthy of the most serious consideration by members of this House. My view of the matter is confirmed by the following quotation from a letter which has been tabled and which is already in Hansard. The letter bears date January 17, 1925, written by the Deputy Minister cf Justice to the Deputy Minister of Public Works in reference to the Montreal, Ottawa and Georgian bay canal, and the last sentence reads:
In any event it seems to me that approval should be withheld unless the work proposed to be constructed will afford traffic and navigation facilities between points which can reasonably be regarded as terminal points of a canal.
That is the opinion of Mr. W. Stuart Edwards, the very capable Deputy Minister of Justice. In other words, he considers that no bill should be passed which would enable the company to develop one or two powers on the Ottawa river without proceeding to the construction of the canal itself.
I am more and more impressed, as I have listened to this debate, with the view that this is a question which should be settled by the two provinces concerned and the Dominion, the parties sitting around a table and coming to a satisfactory conclusion. This is a public matter of the gravest importance, having regard to the respective rights of the provinces and of the Dominion. I know there is considerable difference of opinion about it, and I have no doubt the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), who will follow me, will differ from some of the other lawyers in the House. He will agree .with me, however, that the provinces have some rights on the Ottawa river, just as I am prepared to agree with him that the Dominion also has rights. I do not think these rights are well defined; at least, that is my opinion speaking as a layman. It seems to me that the

only way in which the interest of the people can be safeguarded-because, after all, we are all for the people, whether we be members of a provincial legislature or of the House of Commons-is for the provinces and the Dominion to get together and come to some arrangement regarding the development and the division of water-power on this great river.
Before I sit down I want to say a word in regard to the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Guthrie). When I ventured to oppose the second reading of the bill I had no idea that the newspapers and the public generally would be so keenly interested in the question. I declared then that I was not trying to prevent the bill from going to the committee; I merely wanted to have members of this House as well as the public fully informed regarding the facts. I wanted the members here, before the bill was considered in committee, to be fully seized with the gravity of the situation, more especially in view of the fact that water-power has become an asset of such vital importance to everyone in this country. As I said before, I look forward to the time when our children, or at any rate our grandchildren, will have houses heated with white coal. And that being so it is my opinion that this asset should be retained as far as possible by the people. I think I made it abundantly clear then that I was against the renewal of the charter of the Georgian Bay Canal Company, and as the discussion has proceeded in this House it has become evident that there is a strong feeling in the country that the principle involved in the bill should not be embodied in a private measure. It is a public question which should be dealt with in public legislation. That being the case, and public interest having been aroused as it has been, Rethink the leader of the opposition was quite justified in moving his amendment to the effect that this matter being of a public nature should be dealt with in a public and not in a private bill. Under the circumstances I shall be very glad to support the amendment

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
I do mot rise for the purpose of
either supporting or condemning the merits of the proposed bill, nor do I intend to discuss its expediency. Nor shall I go into the advisability of leasing to private companies the rights of developing power on the Ottawa river, whoever the directors of those companies may be. I shall not even discuss the policy of public ownership, although I may say that while I am not vociferous or fanatical in support of that policy, I have had

Georgian Bay Canal Company
occasion in the past to defend it against some gentlemen who are most violently opposed to the present bill. My purpose in rising is rather to perform what I deem to be my duty.
In the course of this debate, and outside of parliament, voices have been heard pleading and arguing for the rights of the provinces with regard to water-powers in navigable rivers, but so far no voice has been heard asserting the rights of the Dominion government. Without hestitation I have come to the conclusion that it is my duty as a member of the government and as Attorney General for this Dominion to defend the rights of the Dominion government in that respect; I do so the more easily because two years ago, when I occupied my present position, I had occasion to give my opinion on that very subject long before the renewal of this charter was before this House for discussion. In 1925 the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) referred to me a letter which he had received from the premier of the province of Ontario, and asked me what I thought were the respective rights of the federal government and of the provinces with regard to such water-powers. I wrote a letter under date of June 1, 1925, which I desire to now read to the House:
My dear Prime Minister,
Referring to your letter of the 17th ultimo, re. development of additional power at Carillon rapids on the Ottawa river, I may say that ever since the year 1894 the improvement of navigation between Montreal, Ottawa and the Georgian hay has been given earnest consideration by successive administrations, and has formed the subject of parliamentary legislation authorizing the construction of the necessary works. For many reasons, which need not be detailed here, the erection of such works has been postponed from time to time, with the result that no major iniprovement has been made in the navigation-of the Ottawa River. Leases have, however, been already granted covering navigation works at Carillon, one of which was dated the 31st March, 1911, and the other the 1st December, 1921.
With regard to Mr. Ferguson's suggestion that the action of this government should be made dependent upon the consent of the prov-vince of Ontario, my understanding is that any power which may be developed at Carillon will result from the erection of works for the improvement of navigation by or under the authority of the government under the powers conferred upon the Dominion by the British North America Act. Therefore, in so far as any questions regarding the improvement of navigation are concerned, the matter appears to be one in which the Dominion must proceed upon its own responsibility. It may be, however, that in the carrying out of these powers, or in the construction of the proposed works some interest of the province may be affected, and I think therefore that Mr. Ferguson should be informed that this government would welcome any representations which his government
may desire to make upon the subject. So far as I am aware, any interest which the province may have in the matter is of a limited character, depending possibly upon the ownership of lands in the bed of the river or within the area to be flooded. Any interference by the Dominion with such right or interest would form the basis of compensation which might be agreed upon by the governments concerned, but which, in any event, could be determined by adjudication.
T suggest that Mr. Ferguson be informed that so far as the improvement of navigation and the incidental development and disposal of power is concerned, this government is desirous of serving the best interests of Canada, and would be glad to receive any representations or suggestions which the provincial governments may desire to make as to the advisability or otherwise of the proposed scheme, but that this government is unable to recognize any right on the part of the province to control the Dominion in the exercise of its constitutional powers.
Yours faithfully,
Ebnest Lapointe.
This opinion was sent to the Prime Minister after consultation with the officers of the Department of Justice, and was based on opinions given on various occasions by them and by their predecessors in the department.
Reference has been made in the course of this debate to a judgment delivered by the Privy Council in November of the same year, six months after this opinion was given. Let me say, Mr. Speaker, that the judgment of the Privy Council not only says nothing contrary to the opinion then given, but is rather in conformity therewith. I have a copy of that judgment in my hand, delivered in a case between the harbour commissioners of Montreal, the city of Montreal and the government of the province of Quebec. The harbour commissioners of Montreal, acting by virtue of the powers given them by this parliament, had constructed quays and other works and had used for that purpose certain parts of shores of the St. Lawrence river which were declared to be the property of the government of the province of Quebec. Here is what was stated in this judgment:
Now there is no doubt that the power to control navigation and shipping conferred on the Dominion by section 91, is to be widely construed. As was pointed out by Lord Herschell in the judgment which he delivered on behalf of the board in the first of the three fisheries cases .... the terms on which these powers are given are so wide as to be capable of allowing the Dominion parliament to restrict, very seriously the exercise of proprietary rights in a fashion which, to a great extent, depends on the discretion of that parliament. What was said in that case about the enactment of regulations and restrictions in matters relating to fisheries being excluded from the competence of the provincial legislatures applies not less to matters relating to navigation and shipping. But while this is so, it does not appear to their

Any impression that may have been created that the Dominion parliament have no power to authorize the erection of dams in navigable waters is certainly erroneous. The interest which any province can have in the erection of dams in navigable waters is such as it may possess by virtue of its proprietary rights in the bed or the solum, or a certain proprietary interest which it may have in the fisheries. The power to authorize the erection of a dam on any such works is, I claim, exclusively vested in the Dominion parliament; and the only limitation upon the power of the Dominion to expropriate provincial property for the purposes thereof is the limitation mentioned in the judgment of the Privy Council in the harbour commissioners' case, namely, that such power shall not be exercised without compensation. In that case the Privy Council did not decide that the Dominion could not authorize expropriation of provincial crown lands. On the contrary, they decided the opposite. They held in effect, that the particular statutes which authorized the harbour commissioners of Montreal in relation to these works were not effective to vest the provincial lands in question in the 'harbour commissioners unless compensation was paid for them.
Now whatever doubt there might have been as to the effect of that judgment has certainly been dispelled last year in another case which

went to the Privy Council, namely, the reference which was made concerning the application of the Nipissing Central railway to build their line across crown lands of the province of Quebec. An application was made to the governor in council by the Nipissing Central railway, which is really a subsidiary of the railway belonging to the government of the province of Ontario, to be authorized to build their line through the crown lands of the province of Quebec under section 188 of the Railway Act. The province of Quebec took the stand very strongly that this section 188 of the Railway Act was unconstitutional, and that the Dominion government had no right to authorize any Dominion railway to take over lands belonging to the crown in the right of any province of Canada. Reference of this question was made to the Supreme Court of Canada and then to the Privy Council, and the judgment of the Privy Council was along the lines of the judgment which I have alluded to in the case of the harbour commissioners of Montreal. Their Lordships decided that section 188 was perfectly within the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada, and that the Dominion railway authorized by this parliament had the right to take over the lands belonging to the crown in the right of the province, provided they paid compensation for them.
The solum of a river bed is property differing in no essential characteristic from any other lands, so that apart from the question of compensation above referred to, the interest of the province is no greater than that of any private owner of the bed. Now the legislative power of the province to legislate with regard to provincial property is subject to the paramount right of the Dominion to legislate with regard to Dominion property. Mr. Speaker, my purpose
in rising is not to discuss either the merits or the demerits of this particular bill, but rather to draw the attention of the House to what appears to be a very material change in its procedure, and in this connection to the difference between public legislation and private legislation, and the function which parliament was intended to sejrve in reference thereto. Hon. members will, I think, agree that parliament was created primarily for the purpose of enacting measures in the interest of the public generally. Parliament was not created primarily for the purpose of dealing with private legislation. We have only to look at the rules adopted in relation to public and private measures to see how entirely different is the procedure in the two classes of measures.
I need not review the procedure in regard to public bills; it is known and understood by every hon. member in this House. I would, however, draw the attention of parliament to the fact that as respects private legislation there is a material difference. In dealing with private legislation, parliament acts partly in a legislative capacity, partly in a judicial capacity. Before a private bill can come before this House the parties who are interested are required to pay a fee in order to entitle them to have their petition even considered.

Georgian Bay Canal Company
They are obliged to advertise in the public press and in the Canada Gazette with reference to the measure which they intend to present to the House. Before a committee of the House, the parties opposed to them are permitted to appear and to be heard by counsel if so desired. In other words parliament's duty with respect to private legislation is to act partly as a legislative body and partly also as a judicial body. It is apparent that except for most exceptional purposes, the House of Commons collectively is not so constituted as to undertake work of a judicial character. For that reason arrangement is made in the procedure whereby private bills are referred to committees, constituted primarily for the purpose of considering from a judicial point of view whether or not the legislation is of a character which parliament should entertain and pass, and it is for that reason that, with respect to the second reading of private bills, it has never been understood that parliament is passing, excepting conditionally, upon the general principle which is involved in the legislation that is before the House. I think it is important that this should be clearly understood, because if we once permit a departure from the general rule which parliament through its many years of existence had adopted, we shall be establishing a precedent that may be fatal to the progress of legislation in this chamber.
It was on the 25th of February last that the present bill respecting the Georgian bay canal was first discussed in the House. From that day to this on practically every private members' day the time of parliament has been occupied with the discussion of this particular measure. Four full days of the time of parliament have been occupied in the discussion, and the one hour set apart for private legislation has been taken up on eight other different days. On about twelve or thirteen days for the period of time set apart for a consideration of private legislation the time of this House has been exclusively occupied in discussing matters relating to the Georgian bay canal. I contend that of itself that is a sufficient answer as to the propriety of the course which parliament has been taking. It was never intended under any rule of this House that private legislation should occupy such a large part of the time intended to be devoted to public matters by those who were sent to this House to represent the people in reference thereto. The authorities on private and public legislation are in accord in laying down the distinction between the importance to be attached to the second reading of a private bill and 'that to be attached 32649-103-i
to the second reading of a public measure; they make it quite clear that, unless the general principle of a private bill is contrary to the public interest, that bill ought to go to committee, there to be adjudicated on with reference to its expediency.
Now, the general principle of a bill does Dot mean the details of the measure. It does not mean the various matters incidental to the measure; it means simply what the words themselves purport to mean, namely, a broad principle applicable to legislation generally, and equally applicable in one part of the country or another. The general principle to be decided in reference to a private measure is, so to speak, the public morality of the particular measure, whether or not the measure is of a kind that parliament ought to entertain, having regard to its character in a broad way-not the particular application of the measure, not some special feature, not its expediency at a particular time or place, but the broad general principle. Let me illustrate: if a private bill were brought in to license a gambling house, parliament would say at once: "There is here a general principle which we cannot entertain", and the 'bill would be thrown to one side. But if a private bill is brought into the House to give authority to some person to construct an edifice, or a canal, or a work of any particular kind, the principle there is the principle of allowing the construction of the particular kind of device or structure referred to, whatever it may be. If a bill is brought into the House with regard to the licensing of power or the granting of power rights, the general principle there is mot whether rights should be granted to a particular company, not whether rights should be granted at a particular place, but the broad principle whether parliament ought to grant licenses for power, or give power rights at any time or place.
May I quote one or two authorities in support of what I have just said? First of all, I will refer to a statement by Mr. Francis Palgrave, made before a special committee of the British House of Commons as early as the 22nd June, 1832, because it helps to disclose how private legislation has found its way into the discussions of parliament:
The ancient rule as to petitioners for private legislation said Sir Francis Palgrave, was that "no person should come before parliament as a suitor, or trouble parliament if, on the face of his petition, he could have right at home. If there was any other mode of obtaining redress he was not to apply to parliament, but if from the insufficiency of the law or any other similar cause he couid not obtain redress, then the supreme court of parliament was to give

him a speedy and effectual remedy. This course continued until the time of Richard II, when courts of equity were gradually established. The remedial jurisdiction of parliament wholly ceased and was only revived under James I. Private acts of parliament have arisen out of the ancient petition for redress and were formerly called the "Privilegium" because parliament in passing them was considered as granting a privilege. For this reason the committees of the House investigate the facts in each case and report. The House, in reading a private bill for the second time, decides that the matter involved is one which may be looked into by the committee. It is only in case that an exceptional principle is enunciated that the second reading is refused."

May I read one or two other authorities? Sir Courtney Ilbert, late Clerk of the British House of Commons, states:	[DOT]
The proceedings on private bills resemble more closely private litigation between parties interested than a discussion on questions of public policy. The procedure followed for their introduction is different from that provided in the rules for public measures.

Dodd and Wilberforce on Private Bill Procedure at page 20 has the following:
The House does not profess to decide upon the second reading as to the truth or otherwise of the allegations of fact upon which a proposed bill is based, and in conceding a second reading to a private bill the House is regarded as merely giving its sanction to its general principle on the hypothesis that the committee to which it is afterwards referred finds those allegations proved. It is usual, therefore, to allow a second reading, except where the bill enunciates some principle which the House is not prepared to affirm.
If we take the references made by hon. gentlemen opposite as to what the principle of this bill is, up to the present moment no principle has been cited which, as a general principle, this House should not be prepared to recognize one on which a private bill might be considered by a committee.
Let me give a further citation which has an immediate bearing on this bill inasmuch as it refers to a parallel case in the British House of Commons. The Hon. Mr. Lowther, for many years Speaker of the British House, had been before his elevation to that office chairman of committees of the House of Commons, and in that capacity gave more attention to matters of procedure in the House than possibly any other member. As chairman of the committee of ways and means, Mr. Lowther, speaking on February 25, 1896 said:
The rule which the House had generally followed, and he thought very wisely, had been to allow the second reading of private bills to go through unless any strikingly new principle happened to be enunciated therein, and in such cases the House must pause before it accepted the principle. That is taken from the Parliamentary Debates, fourth series, volume 2 37, 1896.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
That is not
the intention. Let me read rule 101 relating to bills and petitions:
Every private bill, when read a second time, is referred to one of the standing committees as follows: bills relating to banks, insurance, trade and commerce, to the committee on Banking and Commerce; bills relating to railways, canals, telegraphs, canal and railway bridges, to the committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines; the bills not coming under these classes to the committee on Miscellaneous Private Bills, and all petitions for or against the bills are considered as referred to such committee.
Inasmuch therefore as this bill has reference to canals it will go to the committee on railways and canals.
In support of my contention that the bill is one concerned with canals, may I, Mr. Speaker, quote your own statement in taking exoeiption to an amendment which was moved by an hon. member on the night of March 21. On that occasion Your Honour made the following assertion:
The purpose of the bill apparently is for the construction of a canal.
And elsewhere:
As a matter of fact the bill is simply for the extension of time for the construction of a canal.
May I say, speaking for myself, that that is the only general principle which I think it is possible properly to apply to this bill: it is a bill relating to the construction of a canal, and as such it should be referred to the committee on railways and canals for adjudication. It will then be for the committee on railways and canals to say whether it is such in fact and whether it is expedient for parlia-

Georgian Bay Canal Company
ment at this particular time to entertain the measure in the form in which it has been sent to them.
Before I conclude I should like to quote the following reference which has been submitted by my hon. friend opposite from his point of view. I desire to quote it in support of my contention. I refer to what Bourinot has to say at page 599, of the fourth edition, in reference to the second reading of private bills:
The second reading corresponds with the same stage in other bills, and in agreeing to it, the House affirms the general principle, or expediency of the measure. There is, however, a distinction between the second reading of a public, and of a private bill, which should not be overlooked. A public bill being founded on reasons of state policy, the House, in agreeing to its second reading, accepts and affirms those reasons; but the expediency of a private bill, being mainly founded upon allegations of fact, which have not yet been proved, the House, in agreeing to its second reading, affirms the principle of the bill, conditionally, and subject to the proof of such allegations before the committee. Where, irrespective of such facts, the principle is objectionable, the House will not consent to the second reading; but otherwise the expediency of the measure is usually left for the consideration of the committee.
I desire to reiterate what I said at the outset. Should the amendment of my hon. friend opposite carry and this bill not be permitted to go to the committee, we shall have established with respect to private bills a new precedent which may become an instrument not only for consuming the time of parliament but for preventing the House from having the opportunity which it should have of dealing with public legislation. More than that, it may become a very powerful instrument for preventing other parties, who have private legislation to be considered by parliament, from ever obtaining a chance for that legislation to be dealt with. We are now, I hope, within measurable distance of the conclusion of the session, and if this debate continues much longer, as it easily can if hon. members are determined to obstruct private legislation, all other persons having private bills to be considered at this session will lose their opportunity entirely. Only by common consent of both sides of the House have a number of private measures gone to the committee. But for the Speaker having taken a generous view of the wishes of the House, and by my hon. friend opposite and myself having agreed at each stage to allow certain measures, which stood on the order paper below' the Georgian bay canal bill, to go to committee, practically the whole of the private legislation of this session would have been held up until the present moment. It
must be apparent that once the precedent is established which it is sought now to create, this parliament is opening the door to a course of procedure which in the future may prove perilous. If persons who are interested in defeating a private measure find a successful method to be that of defeating it on the second reading of the bill in this House and before it goes to a committee, we may expect interests, adverse to other private legislation, to adopt similar methods. It is quite possible that we may find parties interested in defeating private legislation resorting to this method as a means of preventing other legislation from ever being considered by parliament. This method of obstructing the second reading of private bills may be resorted to as a means of preventing not only the particular measure being discussed but any measure subsequently introduced from ever receiving from parliament the consideration it should.
In this particular matter there is involved a wider principle, namely, whether we shall depart from the time-honoured custom of permitting private bills to receive their second reading and to be referred to a committee, conditionally, the understanding being that the committee as a judicial body shall determine whether or not it is expedient, in the light of all the facts and circumstances, for such bills to be favourably reported upon. The question now to be decided is whether we shall recognize and continue that custom, or whether we shall begin a new course of procedure that may affect the whole trend and progress of public business in this House. Let me point out that when thus bill goes to the committee it will be not only the right but that it is the duty of every member freely to exercise his judgment.
There is no commitment of any kind on tne part of the government in resipect to this measure. The government has no interest whatever in this measure apart from having it dealt with as other private bills are dealt with; with as other private bills are dealt with; the government has never had any interest, directly or indirectly, other than to see that all parties who appear here with respect to private legislation are treated alike. Should the bill come back from committee hon. members of this House will be as free as possible to vote as they please with respect to the measure. All I am asking at present, as one who has some responsibility for procedure in this House, is that hon. members consider this vote as one

speakeroldname: Mr. C. H. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St. George):
maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
I desire to take only a few
moments of the time of the House. I think everyone agrees entirely with the authorities cited by the Prime Minister with respect to private bills, and I think the House should deprecate any effort to talk out a bill which is really a private bill, to prevent it from passing simply by an exercise Of the vocal powers of the members on every hour and every day when private bills may be discussed. The House can have only one opinion in that regard. But the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) in the carefully prepared statement which he made to the House to-night, disclosed that there are very grave issues of public policy involved in the subject matter of this discussion.
I do not pretend to give an opinion on the constitutional questions involved. But I have always been under the impression that the provisions of the act of confederation and the schedules thereto, to which the minister made allusion, created prirna facie very strong ground for the argument that the Dominion parliament, having legislative jurisdiction over certain navigable waters, and having legislative jurisdiction with regard to canals at the time of confederation, took over and vested in the crown in the right of the Dominion government not only the canals then in existence but the water-powers then being developed supplementary or ancillary to the construction and operation of these canals, and became vested with the right to utilize these water-powers for hydro-electric purposes; and that when thereafter parliament had undertaken to legislate in regard to canals, and when the government had undertaken to construct Canals, the use of the waters and all rights in and to the hydro-electric power developed as ancillary to the construction of those canals, vested in the Dominion government. There are strong grounds for that contention, and, in view of other matters which will come btfore parliament in the next few years, it is advisable that that issue should Speedily be decided by the highest courts of the country, in order that we may know, in connection with the development not only of the canals on the Ottawa river but the canals on other great rivers whether, having constructed the canals, the crown in the right of the federal government has the property title and interest in and to the hydro electric power thereby developed.

I am disposed to believe that the crown in the right of the Dominion government has that title, and if so we may settle this question of the title to hydro-electric power developed by government canals on navigable streams in a way which will not be in accord with the contentions of the provincial governments of Ontario and Quebec. That being so, and that question of title having been raised in relation to this bill, both by the legislature and government of Ontario and the legislature and government of Quebec, it is clearly apparent that this .bill involves questions of grave public policy. I would be the last .to attempt to prevent in any direct or indirect way any private bill from going before ithe standing committee which has power to investigate its merits and hear the evidence of the parties concerned; but, in respect of this bill, the moment the issue arose that it involved grave questions of public policy, questions concerning which the legislatures and governments of Ontario and Quebec had taken a strong stand, then it became the duty of this government to assume full responsibility in the matter and either to request the promoters of this bill to withdraw it for the time being or, with full knowledge of the issues involved, for the Prime Minister, as the leader of the House, from his place in the House to rise and take full responsibility for the measure, and ask that it be placed upon the public orders as a government measure. In view of the issues which are involved it would be wrong for this House any longer to regard this as purely a private bill involving nothing more than is involved in the ordinary private bill coming before the House. That is my opinion about it.
The Prime Minister has stated that on some twelve or thirteen occasions similar bills have been before the House and have passed the second reading and been sent to committee. All I can say in that regard is that the issues which are raised to-day were not raised on any of those occasions, and, if these issues had been raised by the governments of the two adjoining provinces on any previous occasion, it would then have become apparent that grave matters of public policy were involved, and, in fulfilling its due .responsibility of guarding the public estate which is vested in the crown in the right of the Dominion government, the government would not have-allowed the bill to go before the committee-on private bills. As soon as a private bill clearly takes on the aspect of a public bill, just so soon should all the rules with regard to -public bills apply, and just so soon should

Georgian Bay Canal Company
the government assume the responsibility of dealing with it as a public bill. That is my view of the question.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. D. EULER (Minister of Customs and Excise):
maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I should apologize to the House for rising after the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) had apparently closed the debate. I may also say that I do not propose to answer the more or less constitutional argument advanced by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan). This bill being a private measure, I should like to state very clearly at the outset that I am speaking not as a member of the government but rather as the representative of a constituency which takes a very keen interest in the principle of public ownership. If I may be pardoned for making the reference, I might say that the constituency of North Waterloo, which I have the honour to represent, is the birthplace of the great hydro electric enterprise in the province of Ontario. The men who initiated that enterprise-which I think is the outstanding successful example of a great public utility-the men who initiated that enterprise in a practical way were men from the constituency of North Waterloo, and it was in the city of Kitchener, in that constituency, that the power from Niagara was officially inaugurated. And so Kitchener was a leader in the initiation and use of Niagara power in the province of Ontario The city of Kitchener has been very successful along other lines in the conduct of public utilities under public ownership; and it was because of that, and for other reasons, that a good many years ago I became convinced that the great majority of public services upon which depend the convenience and the prosperity of the people in general ought to be owned and controlled by the people themselves. In that I also include the development of some of our natural resources such as, for example, the development ol water-powers on our great rivers.
The bill under discussion touches that principle at two points; that of the construction of the canal, and the development of the water-powers following upon the construction of the canal. So far as I am concerned I would oppose the bill itself on both counts. If it is indeed feasible, which I very much doubt-I doubt whether the Georgian bay canal can be constructed-I would say that when the time comes when it ought to be constructed it should be built by the people of Canada themselves. But the matter of power, I think, is at the moment of more importance than the canal; and I would regard it as almost unthinkable in these days, with
the advancement that has been made in the development of water-powers, in the province of Ontario at least, that the control and ownership of such powers should be placed in private hands. I also realize the difficulty with regard to the matter of public ownership with regard to the powers on the Ottawa river. As it happens, our friends in the province of Quebec-and I have no fault to find with them at all-are not so favorable to the principle of public ownership as we are in the province of Ontario, but I would make this suggestion:	that since the Dominion undoubtedly has rights on the Ottawa, and as both provinces undoubtedly have rights on that river, it is advisable, and I think feasible, that a conference should be held between the three governments for the purpose of arriving at a satisfactory settlement of the various rights and to decide upon an equitable arrangement with regard to the powers on that river. You might have several solutions, and I want to advance one which has not yet been mentioned in this House: it might conceivably be decided at such a conference that it would be in the public interest that some private company should be given the development of these power rights. I do not think that would follow; I hope it would not. It might be decided between the provinces that they could get together and in a publicly-owned enterprise develop the powers on the Ottawa river. And then there is this further suggestion I should like to make, although it may be regarded as impracticable. The Dominion government has undoubted navigation rights on the Ottawa river, and I have been informed that it would be a not very expensive undertaking to canalize the Ottawa river from Carillon down to the St. Lawrence-that it would cost very little. In connection with that development several hundred thousand horse-power could be secured, and it might be regarded as a very good solution of the whole problem if the Dominion government developed the power, and then sold it to the Ontario hydro commission and to those in the province of Quebec who might desire to purchase.

much to precedent. We have first, second and third reading of a bill, and of a resolution, and the same thing takes place in the Senate. Mr. Speaker, I am sure you, Sir, as well as many other members of the House, must be much impressed with the spectacle which we have witnessed to-night in the belated statement of the position of the government in regard to this bill. The first minister to speak, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe)

Georgian Bay Canal Company
reviewed at considerable length the constitutional feature of the bill. But I will draw to the attention of the House the fact that his whole argument was based upon the premise that we were discussing the question of the right of the Dominion government to deal with matters pertaining to navigable waters. The whole of his citations, his own learned judgment or statement of his opinion, the statements from the Privy Council, the Supreme Court of Canada and the Privy Council again, all referred to matters having to do with navigable waters. No person on this side of the House or, indeed, in the House, has argued that this parliament has not the absolute right to deal with measures pertaining to navigable waters. What those on this side who have taken the constitutional question in hand argue is that this bill is as a matter of fact a deceitful measure. It is given to this House as a measure for the construction of a canal, when every hon. member knows-and all who have spoken except the hon. member fathering the bill acknowledge it-that it is in fact a measure for the promotion of waterpower development, an altogether different proposition. None of the citations of the Minister of Justice dealt with that feature of the case.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) who followed, spent practically all his time in an effort to establish the principle of sending this bill to a committee of the House and to impress upon the House and the country that it was the duty of the House to send the bill to a committee; that the House had no real choice in the matter; that if we did not do that we would violate some cherished principle of constitutional and popular government. As a matter of fact all the rules pertaining to this subject, every citation he made, as well as the practice of this House and of the British House, are to the effect that the Second reading is the occasion upon which, if we have an objection to the principle of a bill, that objection should be registered.
Not only is that the case, but according to our rules governing private bills, if this bill goes to the select committee, that committee have no power to alter the principle of the bill. That committee cannot vary the nature of the bill from what was sent to them by this House. With the consent of the promoters of the bill they may vary it to some extent; but if they do so, they must report the variations to the House. Furthermore, that committee are not permitted to follow the suggestion made by the Minister of Customs (Mr. Euler) namely to kill the bill. By the rules of the House they are specifically precluded from delaying or in any other
way killing the bill. They must report the bill to the House. It is infinitely more of an invasion of the rights of the citizens of Canada, which rights were referred to so touchingly by the Prime Minister, to refuse to report the bill to the House than to refuse to send the bill to committee. What I want to impress upon the minds of every hon. member who has been arguing on this point is that the committee have no right to vary the principle of the bill; they have no right to curtail the powers contained in the bill, and they must report the bill to the House. They have no right by underhand methods to assassinate the bill, as has been suggested by the Minister of Customs.

Yes. We know perfectly
well the Minister of Customs is absolutely opposed to the bill. We knew that before he said so. We know perfectly well that his judgment-and it is a judgment of a very sound character-is wholly against the principle of the bill, and this is the time when he ought to vote against that principle. I will venture to say this to the minister:	If
he had taken that stand when the government were talking this matter over and had told his colleagues that he as a member of the government would oppose the bill as his conscience and judgment dictated, the government would not be standing behind the bill to-night. They would not dare to do so because, being divided on the question, they could not face this House. To escape the dilemma the Minister of Customs says that he will vote for the second reading, but with the distinct understanding that this bill will go to a committee where it is to be given an underhand death, smothered to death,

Georgian Bay Canal Company
strangled in the dark somehow. That is not, I submit, consistent with my hon. friend's usual courage. No, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member and those who think like him ought to vote against this measure on the second reading, when the principle of the bill is under consideration and being decided.
In regard to the bill itself, I have already stated that the reason I object to it is that, on the face of it, it is a piece of sham and deceit. There is not a member of this House, with the exception of my hon. friend who promoted or who is fathering 'the bill in the House-and to him I will come in a moment- who has asserted that this bill is for the purpose of constructing a canal. Every hon. member who has spoken-and I have followed the debate with care-has emphasized the power feature of this bill. Furthermore, it is known to everyone in the House that this canal would never be built by Sir Clifford Sifton and his associates if they were shorn of the rights to take the power incidental to such development. It is clear, Mr. Speaker, that this is a power bill and not a canal bill.
In the second place, I make the point that if the canal were to be constructed, assuming that they would construct the canal, it is calculated and intended that any cost of that construction shall be borne by moneys raised on the power feature of the bill. What does that mean? It means that whatever power is developed out of that one million and a quarter horse-power on this waterway will have to bear, in addition to the cost of the power, the cost of the canal. In other words, such power cannot and never will be developed and sold to the public at as low a price as would be the case if it were a purely power project. That is a feature which we should take cognizance of, and if we put our imprimatur on the principle of the second reading of the measure we as a parliament are approving, or at least those who vote for it, of that proceeding.
The point was raised by my hon. friend who is fathering the bill in the House that there might be compensation features in case the crown desired to take over the work. I have the clause under my hand. This again is a reason why we should reject the measure. We know the canal is not to be constructed; every hon. member is cognizant of that fact. And if we support the principle of the bill and we invoke clause 5 of the act of 1906-section 43 of the original act what do we let the government and the country in for? That section provides that His Majesty, his heirs and successors, may assume the possession of this property, and by way of compensation shall pay to the company the value of the work

actually done by the company up to the time of the giving of such notice, the making of plans, the cost and value of the plants and otherwise upon the ground; together with the value of all tangible property of the company. Everything that the company has, including the charter, its plans, its plants, its expenses to date-all must 'be paid for. We must compensate them for all these things and the value of the power incidental to it. Already, according to the brief brought to this House by my hon. friend from Ottawa, we find that the company expect to develop very large quantities of electrical energy. Does any hon. gentleman in this House, much less a member of the government, who has had experience in this matter suggest for a moment that there will not 'be a claim for compensation for the relinquishment of the power? They declare that if they get this charter through they will have absolute control of the waterpower on these waterways amounting, we are told to some million and a quarter horse-power -one of the most valuable franchises ever given to a private interest in the history of Canada. That is a pretty broad statement, but I will venture to repeat it; that we are at this moment about to vote on one of the most valuable franchises ever given to any private interest in the history of this country. And what is the country to get in return for it? Absolutely nothing. There is not within the confines of the bill a single provision to give any return to the country for this stupendous franchise.
My hon. friend from Dauphin (Mr. Ward) this evening sought to justify the stand that he has taken, and I desire to point out to him the rather anomalous position in which he finds himself. I want to impress upon him and upon other hon. members the danger of supporting the measure or voting for the second reading. It is all very well to say we can explain it away to those who are not familiar with parliamentary practice, but the fact of the matter is that we are voting for a principle and we are voting for the approval of this bill when we vote on the second reading. My hon. friend said this evening that he would suggest the erection of a federal hydro-electric commission to take over the water-powers on all our rivers and streams in Canada. Then he complained .that Manitoba was being exploited to-day by the lease which he said this government had made to some private interests on the Nelson river. Let him follow me for a moment. He complains because the Interior department had given a lease-I never heard of it, by the way-of water-power on the Nelson river in Manitoba, and that the people of Manitoba have been

Georgian Bay Canal Company
deprived of their rights. If such a lease has been given I agree with him. But what is he doing to-night? He is voting to deprive the provinces of Quebec and Ontario of a similar right. It is true that the wiater-powers and natural resources of Manitoba do not' constitutionally belong to the people of Manitoba; still he complains because in the administration of the water-powers of Manitoba this government is depriving the people of Manitoba of any say in their development. Yet by his vote to-night, he will attempt to deprive Quebec and Ontario of the very right which he complains they are being deprived of in Manitoba.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext: Will my hon. friend explain to this House-I am seeking for information -just how the water-powers of the Ottawa river are to be developed under the circumstances I pictured in my remarks?

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext: I cannot recall in detail the circumstances pictured by my hon. friend, but there is no difficulty in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec coming to an understanding regarding the development of water-power on their rivers or on bordering rivers. Furthermore, we have the premiers of both provinces telling this government-not telling the government, but through Mr. Speaker telling the House-that they object to this parliament usurping the powers and rights which they in each province claim for their own. That is before us officially, and can we not trust these two premiers and their governments to make their own arrangements? They are not children; they do not require the federal government to make arrangements for them. It is their right, it is their power, they claim it, and no constitutional argument has been put forward to-night or at any other time to successfully combat their claim. So I submit they will work out that problem themselves.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext: Is it not a fact, and has it not been stated in this House repeatedly, that the water of the Ottawa river belongs to the people of Canada?

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
No. The only claim the Dominion government makes to the water of the Ottawa river is for navigation purposes. For instance the right of diversion for waterworks or for electric energy belongs to the provinces. Even the fish in the river belong to the provinces. There is no question about that. The bed of the river also. belongs to the provinces. The only right the Dominion has is, ae I have said, the right regarding navigation. I say again, Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that this is not a navigation bill. That, is the point we make. The government
takes the position that this is a navigation bill. They know it is not. My right hon. friend knows perfectly well that Sir Clifford Sifton will never come before this government and seriously ask for authority to construct a canal for navigation purposes short of excess water-power, never in the wide world. The whole House knows that this is not a navigation scheme, a canal scheme. It is a power scheme, the most gigantic ever conceived in Canada up to this time, under the guise of and falsified as a canal scheme.
Now my hon. friend the sponsor of this bill said to the House the other day-and this is where I made the exception a moment ago-[DOT] that no power was to be sold except the surplus which might be developed over the needs of the canal. Again I want to point to the deception of that statement. I do not mean that in a discourteous or unparliamentary sense. I mean in so far as those behind the bill are concerned, the promoters; it is their deception to which I refer. And this is the deception: they come to parliament asking for a right which was granted in 1894, when the generation of hydro-electric energy was problematical; it was not a demonstrated commercial success for long afterwards. At that time they secured under their charter the right to the surplus power-surplus power which then and for many years afterwards had no value and no significance, and which meant very little to any person in this country except a few perhaps with vision. But to-day electrical energy is of primary and paramount importance to the people of Canada, especially the people of Ontario and Quebec in the territory adjacent to these water-powers. The very industrial life of these two provinces is dependent upon the future development of hydro-eleotric energy. Therefore I come to what my hon. friend said when in the course of his speech he sought to lead the House into this state of mind: Well, they were only getting a mere bagatelle, just the surplus power. As a matter of fact the power required for the canal would be a mere modicum of the power possible of development. I venture this statement, Mr. Speaker, that the 250 horse-power now being developed at Carillon would be ample to run the canal or even a larger work for all time to come. But we are told they can develop three or four hundred thousand horse-power, and it would be this surplus that they would have to sell to the public. We contend that this is not fair to the people of these two provinces or to the country as a whole.
Now I wish to say a word or two regarding the bill itself. I have all the various bills

Georgian Bay Canal Company
under my hand, and I notice that in every one of them the list of directors is set forth; but I call the attention of the government and of the House to this significant fact, that by section 2, cf the bill now before the House, to which we are about to give second reading, the section in the 1924 act which sets up the directorate is repealed, and if passed this bill will leave the company without any directorate at all so far as the records show. We have asked who are the directors. I want to ask the government:	Do they know who are
the directors of this concern? Surely this company is of sufficient importance that the House should be at least advised whom they are incorporating or re-incorporating. Who are to be the directors? Who are the people that are asking for this bill? It is not set out in the bill before us. It is deliberately deleted from the bill.
Furthermore, as my hon. friend from Argen-teuil (Sir George Perley) very properly pointed out this evening, all this company has to do is to start development at, say, the two largest water-powers on the waterway, one I understand at Carillon and the other farther up the river this side of Mattawa-I do not know the exact name-where I am told they can develop three or four hundred thousand horse-power; indeed one person told me the potential development is six hundred thousand horse-power. Supposing the promoters take possession of these two spots, commence their work under this charter-if it is given to them. They need not build a single foot of waterway on either side of these powers. All they need do is simply to develop the waterway at those points, take possession of the water-powers and utilize them, and then tell the government:	You can have the rest of the
canal if you want it. That is the principle of the bill. I say to the Prime Minister that under the rules of the House if this bill goes to the committee it will not be competent for the committee to vary the bill in these respects to any great extent, except with the consent of the promoters. I am quite sure that they will never consent to deletion of the right to develop hydro-electric power.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
May I ask
my hon. friend this question: if it were to appear to the committee that the company were seeking to get powers which were not granted under its original charter, would not that be a sufficient ground for the committee to report against the House accepting the bill?

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
Yes; but I want to point out to the Prime Minister that these powers are in the original charter. That is the right

they have, as my hon. friend who sponsors the bill very properly pointed out. I cannot put my finger on the clause, but the original charter gives the company the right _ to take power in addition to that needed for the canal, and this right has been continued down to the present time. They can only sell power in excess of that required for the canal. Of course, that is ordinary common sense; but they are entitled to that power. How are their tolls fixed? By the railway board. That is in the original charter, and that is what we are quarrelling with. When the original charter was secured this power was valueless, it was a mere incident to the canal and was not considered of any importance at all. But during recent years, particularly during the last ten years, and more particularly during the last five years, the demand for power has become such that it is a subject of paramount importance, and the canal sinks into insignificance in relation to the value of the power. And that is the reason, if I may impress this upon the mind of the Prime Minister, why we are so bitterly opposed to the bill. It is not to stop genuine private interests from going to a committee, not at all; it is to prevent private interests securing a right under the guise of promoting something altogether different from what they are attempting to secure,

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
Under the charter as
granted would it be possible for these people to develop power without building the canal?

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext: Yes, certainly.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext: Certainly not.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
My hon. friend has just
taken his seat. A moment ago I pointed out that the promoters can build a canal at Carillon falls with the necessary dam and locks. They would, incidentally to that worfcj develop from 200,000 to 400,000 horse-power. They could go up the river this side of Mattawa and there construct a dam, together with the necessary locks, and develop, I am told, from 300.000 to 600,000 horse-power more, and nothing in this bill now before us would oblige them to complete the waterway in between. Let me read what is here proposed:
The company may commence the construction of its canals, or any of them.
I want the House to bear those few words in mind. This is not a canal; it is a series of canals; it is not a specific work, but a whole chain of works. They may construct its canals or any of them before a certain time:
And if such construction is not commenced and such expenditure is not so made, or if the said canals are not completed and put in opera-

Georgian Bay Canal Company
tion within the said periods respectively, the powers granted to the company by parliament shall cease and be null and void as respects so much of the said canals and works as then remains uncompleted.
The powers shall be null and void-to what extent? As respects that portion of the works and canals that remains uncompleted. The language is as clear as it could possibly be, and the intent of the promoters is equally obvious.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext: Judging from what- my hon. friend has read, is it not a fact that the power developed, either on the whole of the works or on any section thereof, will always be incidental to the completion of the whole canal or of any section of it?

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
Certainly. The power at
these falls will be incidental, if you like to make it so.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext: It has to be.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext: But what we claim is that these dams ought to be constructed for the purpose of power and not ostensibly for the purposes of the canal. In other words, we say that these promoters are coming before parliament with a deceptive measure. They come before us with unclean hands. They are seeking to deceive parliament, although I am ready to admit that parliament is not deceived. If you give the second reading to this bill you put the stamp of approval on the effort of the company to deceive this House and conceal what their real intent is.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext: Will the hon. member pardon another interruption? This will be my last question. Am I to understand that my hon. friend would not be against the bill if it were really what it purports to be, and if the House were not deceived by it?

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
Yes, I would be against the bill in any case, and I will tell the hon. gentleman why. I may anticipate his next question, which he will not ask, seeing that the one he has just put he said would be his last. His next question would be, "Why have you voted for this measure during the last sixteen or seventeen years?" As a matter of fact I do not know that I always did vote for it, because it has always been a question with me; but I may state the reason why I would oppose it now in any case. I am speaking from memory and am therefore subject to correction, but I think I may safely say that during the past thirteen or fourteen years, two groups of experts, one appointed by the government from its own staff, and the other under Mr. Sanford Evans, have made a most exhaustive examination of this whole canal project, and
the last report of Mr. Sanford Evans was submitted about the year 1920 or 1922. I am not sure about the exact date, but in any case the report was brought down a few years ago, and in both instances these experts declared that in their opinion the canal scheme was not feasible. Until that time it was problematical whether it was or not, but that was their report. My own conviction is that, even if it were a straight canal scheme, it is not feasible.
I do not think it is worth my time to go into other reasons for rejecting this measure. I could cite other and very sound reasons, but that is not necessary. The canal feature of the bill is not argued in this House as an excuse for passing it, and I venture to say you would not get half a dozen members here to vote for the measure on the strength of the canal proposal. I have not heard a single member, apart from the hon. gentleman who has fathered the bill, who did not emphasize the power aspect of the project. I would not vote for the bill on either ground. But, to repeat myself, I am opposing it because, under the guise of a proposal to build a canal on this worn out charter, the bill seeks to obtain control of a million and a quarter horse-power, and is therefore the largest, the most significant and the most valuable franchise ever sought by a single corporation in the history of Canada.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
Just for a few moments I want to indicate to the House what is involved in this matter. I want to point out what we are giving away in this bill and contrast that with the development that has taken place on the Niagara river. About the very time that this company came before parliament another company approached the Ontario government with a proposal to develop power at Niagara Falls. The House will be interested to know that the Ontario government gave to that company, an English concern, a contract for the development in perpetuity of all the power at Niagara Falls for the sum of $25,000 per annum. That, I say, was about the time that the present company came on the scene on the Ottawa river to build a canal. At that time the transmission of electrical energy was not known, and this English company, not being able to transmit any power, were forced to abandon the contract. There is now being transmitted in electrical current on the Niagara river at Niagara Falls over 1,000,000 horse-power, an amount equal to the horsepower that may be developed on the Ottawa, Does this House know what the province of Ontario is doing in addition to the development of hydro? That province, apart from

Georgian Bay Canal Company
what it is doing for the people of Ontario and of Canada, is paying a rental of $500,000 per annum to the parks commission for the upkeep of the parks of the province. In other words, this power which we are giving away is worth at least the amount which the Ontario government is paying to its parks commission. The power on the Ottawa river as a rental proposition is valued at $1,000,000 per annum. Is this government as a government going to overlook such a condition? Are hon. gentlemen opposite not continuing a pretty good franchise to their friends at $1,000,000 a year? I want to ask this government whether the Sifton family have not had enough out of the country. Is it not time that some of these gentlemen of the west, who know something of this group, realized that this government has no right to give them any more?

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext: This government is backing the proposition. We have found that out now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
I am glad my
hon. friend has made that statement because it is the insinuation which hon. gentlemen opposite have thrown out repeatedly in the course of this debate. I wish to make it absolutely clear that the government is in no way committed to the project, nor has it been so committed at any time directly or indirectly. This is a private bill in which the government has no interest other than to see that it is treated as other private bills are treated, and any remarks to the contrary are entirely false and unwarranted.

In reply to the Prime
Minister I would say that all he has to do to prove his words is to take off the whip and let the House decide the matter on division.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

I again rise
to a point of order, I ask whether or not t'he remark just made by the hon. gentleman, in view of what I have already said, is in order, and whether he should not be called upon to retract it?

(Mr. Chaplin.]
does he mean by "taking off the whip?" I do not know; the 'Speaker does not know what the hon. gentleman meant, and until I do know what is meant I cannot rule.

maintopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY

accept the word of the Prime Minister, but I simply ask him to take off the whip.
